cards.title: Physical Quantities and SI Units — Worked Example
points: Example: What are the SI base units for length, mass, and time?
Step 1: Length is measured in metres (m).
Step 2: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg).
Step 3: Time is measured in seconds (s).
Answer: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s)

cards.title: Physical Quantities and SI Units — Worked Example
points: Example: The Newton (N) is a derived unit. Express it in terms of SI base units.
Step 1: Force = mass × acceleration (F = ma).
Step 2: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg).
Step 3: Acceleration is measured in m/s².
Step 4: So N = kg × m/s² = kg·m/s².
Answer: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²

cards.title: Density — How Tightly Packed is the Mass?
points: Explanation: **Density means:** how much stuff is inside a certain amount of space.
More to know: That is all.
Definition: Density is the **mass per unit volume** of a substance.

cards.title: Density — How Tightly Packed is the Mass? — Worked Example
points: Example: A block of wood has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 300 cm³. Calculate its density.
Step 1: __computation__
Answer: ρ = 0.8 g/cm³ (or 800 kg/m³)

cards.title: Density — How Tightly Packed is the Mass? — Worked Example
points: Example: An irregular stone has a mass of 150 g. When placed in a measuring cylinder of water, the water level rises from 50 cm³ to 80 cm³. Find the density of the stone.
Step 1: __computation__
Answer: ρ = 5 g/cm³ (or 5000 kg/m³)

cards.title: Scalars and Vectors — Magnitude and Direction — Worked Example
points: Example: A force of 6 N acts east, and a force of 8 N acts north. Find the resultant force.
Step 1: Draw a right-angled triangle with 6 cm east and 8 cm north.
Step 2: The resultant is the hypotenuse.
Step 4: Direction = tan⁻¹(8/6) = 53.1° north of east.
Answer: 10 N at 53.1° north of east

cards.title: Scalars and Vectors — Magnitude and Direction — Worked Example
points: Example: A boy walks 3 km east, then 4 km south. What is his displacement from the starting point?
Step 1: Draw a right-angled triangle with 3 km east and 4 km south.
Step 2: Resultant = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 km.
Step 3: Direction = tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1° south of east.
Answer: 5 km at 53.1° south of east

cards.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance — The Basics of Circuits
points: More to know: These quantities describe what pushes the charge, how much charge flows, and how strongly the circuit opposes that flow.

cards.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance — The Basics of Circuits — Worked Example
points: Example: A resistor has a voltage of 12 V across it and a current of 2 A flowing through it. Calculate its resistance.
Step 1: Voltage (V) = 12 V.
Step 2: Current (I) = 2 A.
Step 3: Resistance (R) = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 Ω.
Answer: R = 6 Ω

cards.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance — The Basics of Circuits — Worked Example
points: Example: A circuit has a resistance of 10 Ω and a voltage of 230 V. Calculate the current.
Step 1: Voltage (V) = 230 V.
Step 2: Resistance (R) = 10 Ω.
Step 3: Current (I) = V ÷ R = 230 ÷ 10 = 23 A.
Answer: I = 23 A

cards.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance — The Basics of Circuits — Worked Example
points: Example: A lamp transfers 240 J of energy when 20 C of charge passes through it. Calculate the voltage.
Step 1: Energy (W) = 240 J.
Step 2: Charge (Q) = 20 C.
Step 3: Voltage (V) = W ÷ Q = 240 ÷ 20 = 12 V.
Answer: V = 12 V

cards.title: Voltage, Current, and Resistance — The Basics of Circuits — Worked Example
points: Example: A current of 3 A flows for 4 seconds. Calculate the charge transferred.
Step 1: Current (I) = 3 A.
Step 2: Time (t) = 4 s.
Step 3: Charge (Q) = I × t = 3 × 4 = 12 C.
Answer: Q = 12 C

o-level/form-3/physics/MechanicalStructu.title: Mechanical Structures
snippets: Simple span with supports at ends
Arch Bridge Load carried by curved arch in compression
Cables and towers support the deck
Supported by piers along the span

cards.title: Beams — Supporting Loads Across a Span — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain why an I-beam is stronger than a solid rectangular beam of the same mass.
Step 1: An I-beam has material concentrated at the top and bottom flanges, where stress is highest.
Step 2: This gives a high second moment of area (resistance to bending) without adding extra mass.
Step 3: The web connects the flanges and resists shear forces.
Answer: An I-beam has a better strength-to-weight ratio because material is placed where it is most effective.

cards.title: Beams — Supporting Loads Across a Span — Worked Example
points: Example: A simply supported beam AB is 5 m long. A point load of 200 N is applied 3 m from support A. Find the reaction force at support B.
Step 1: Take moments about A: W × distance from A = R_B × L
Answer: R_B = 120 N

cards.title: Beams — Supporting Loads Across a Span — Worked Example
points: Example: Using the beam in the previous question, find the reaction force at support A.
Step 1: R_A + R_B = W
Answer: R_A = 80 N

cards.title: Beams — Supporting Loads Across a Span — Worked Example
points: Example: A cantilever beam is fixed into a wall at one end. Explain what happens to the free end when a load is added, and why the fixed end must be strong.
Step 1: The free end has no support, so it bends downward under the load.
Step 2: All of the bending force must be carried by the fixed end alone, since there is no second support to share it.
Step 3: This means the fixed end experiences the largest stresses in the whole beam.
Answer: The free end droops, and the fixed end must resist all the bending on its own.

cards.title: Trusses — The Power of Triangles — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain why triangles are used in truss construction.
Step 1: A triangle is rigid — it cannot change its shape without changing the length of one of its sides.
Step 2: This means that a triangular frame stays in shape under load, making it a stable structural element.
Step 3: Rectangles, by contrast, can easily deform into parallelograms.
Answer: Triangles are used because they are inherently rigid and maintain their shape under load.

cards.title: Trusses — The Power of Triangles — Worked Example
points: Example: In a roof truss, the top chord is in compression and the bottom chord is in tension. What does this mean?
Step 1: The top chord is being pushed together (compressed) by the weight of the roof and any loads on it.
Step 2: The bottom chord is being pulled apart (stretched) as it resists the outward thrust from the top chord.
Step 3: The diagonals may be in either tension or compression depending on their orientation.
Answer: Top chord = compression (strut), bottom chord = tension (tie).

cards.title: Trusses — The Power of Triangles — Worked Example
points: Example: What is the advantage of a truss over a solid beam for a bridge?
Step 1: A truss uses less material than a solid beam for the same span and load capacity.
Step 2: This makes the structure lighter and more economical.
Step 3: The open framework also reduces wind resistance and allows for easier inspection.
Answer: Trusses provide a better strength-to-mass ratio, using less material to achieve the same strength.

cards.title: Trusses — The Power of Triangles — Worked Example
points: Example: A triangular roof truss rests on two supports, A and B, 8 m apart. A load of 240 N acts on a joint 3 m from A. Find R_B.
Step 1: Take moments about A: W × distance from A = R_B × L
Answer: R_B = 90 N

cards.title: Joining Materials — Connecting Parts Together — Worked Example
points: Example: Why is a glued joint with a large contact area stronger than a joint with a small contact area?
Step 1: A larger contact area allows the adhesive to spread the load over a greater surface.
Step 2: This reduces the stress per unit area on the glue line.
Step 3: The joint is less likely to fail under load.
Answer: Larger contact area distributes load better and reduces stress on the adhesive.

cards.title: Joining Materials — Connecting Parts Together — Worked Example
points: Example: Compare pinning and welding as methods for joining steel beams.
Step 1: Pinning uses bolts or rivets — it is quick and allows for disassembly, but may have stress concentrations at the holes.
Step 2: Welding fuses the metal — it creates a continuous, very strong joint but requires skill and cannot be easily undone.
Step 3: Welded joints are generally stronger for permanent structures.
Answer: Welding creates a stronger, continuous joint; pinning allows for disassembly but may have stress concentrations.

cards.title: Joining Materials — Connecting Parts Together — Worked Example
points: Example: Why are dowels sometimes used with glued joints in woodwork?
Step 1: Dowels add mechanical strength to the joint — they resist shear forces.
Step 2: They also help align the pieces correctly during assembly.
Step 3: The combination of glue (bonding) and dowels (mechanical strength) gives a very strong joint.
Answer: Dowels add mechanical strength and alignment to glued joints.

cards.title: Joining Materials — Connecting Parts Together — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain the difference between a temporary joint and a permanent joint, giving one example of each.
Step 1: A temporary joint, such as a bolt and nut, can be undone without damaging the parts.
Step 2: A permanent joint, such as a weld, cannot be separated without destroying the joint or the material.
Step 3: The choice depends on whether the parts will ever need to be taken apart again.
Answer: Temporary joints (e.g. bolts) can be disassembled; permanent joints (e.g. welds) cannot.

o-level/form-3/physics/Optics.title: Optics
snippets: i r Incident ray Refracted ray Normal Light bends towards the normal Light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium (glass), and away from the normal when entering a less dense medium (air).

i r Incident ray Reflected ray Interface i > c → total internal reflection When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, all light is reflected back into the denser medium — total internal reflection.
Parallel rays converge at focus Diverging (Concave) Lens

cards.title: Reflection of Light — Laws and Plane Mirrors
points: Explanation: **Reflection** occurs when light bounces off a surface. The laws of reflection govern how light behaves when it strikes a smooth, shiny surface like a mirror.
More to know: The **laws of reflection** state: (1) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r). (2) The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.

cards.title: Reflection of Light — Laws and Plane Mirrors — Worked Example
points: Example: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
Step 1: According to the law of reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Step 2: i = 30°, so r = 30°.
Answer: r = 30°

cards.title: Reflection of Light — Laws and Plane Mirrors — Worked Example
points: Example: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a plane mirror. How far behind the mirror is the image?
Step 1: For a plane mirror, the image distance equals the object distance.
Step 2: Object distance = 20 cm, so image distance = 20 cm behind the mirror.
Answer: Image is 20 cm behind the mirror.

cards.title: Reflection of Light — Laws and Plane Mirrors — Worked Example
points: Example: Describe the characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror.
Step 1: The image is virtual (cannot be projected).
Step 2: It is the same size as the object.
Step 3: It is laterally inverted (left–right reversed).
Step 4: It is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Answer: Virtual, same size, laterally inverted, same distance behind as object in front.

cards.title: Refraction — Bending Light
points: Explanation: **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in speed. When light enters a denser medium, it bends towards the normal; when it enters a less dense medium, it bends away from the normal.
More to know: The amount of bending is described by the **refractive index (n)** of the material. Snell's Law relates the angles of incidence and refraction: sin i / sin r = n.

cards.title: Refraction — Bending Light — Worked Example
points: Example: A ray of light enters a glass block from air. If the angle of incidence is 45° and the angle of refraction is 28°, calculate the refractive index of the glass.
Answer: n ≈ 1.51

cards.title: Refraction — Bending Light — Worked Example
points: Example: The critical angle for a glass-air boundary is 42°. What is the refractive index of the glass?
Answer: n ≈ 1.49

cards.title: Refraction — Bending Light — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain why a straw in a glass of water appears bent.
Step 1: Light from the straw travels from water (denser) to air (less dense).
Step 2: The light bends away from the normal at the water-air interface.
Step 3: Our eyes perceive the light as coming from a straight line, giving the illusion that the straw is bent.
Answer: Refraction of light at the water-air surface causes the straw to appear bent.

cards.title: Lenses — Converging and Diverging
points: Explanation: A **lens** is a transparent optical device that refracts light to form an image. There are two main types: **converging (convex)** lenses and **diverging (concave)** lenses.
More to know: A converging lens brings parallel rays of light together at a focal point. A diverging lens spreads parallel rays apart.

cards.title: Lenses — Converging and Diverging — Worked Example
points: Example: A converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. Describe the image formed.
Step 1: Object distance u = 30 cm (beyond focal length).
Step 2: A real, inverted image will be formed on the other side of the lens.
Step 3: Since u > f, it forms a real image.
Answer: Real, inverted image (could be used in a camera or projector).

cards.title: Lenses — Converging and Diverging — Worked Example
points: Example: An object is placed 5 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. What type of image is formed?
Step 1: Object distance u = 5 cm, which is less than focal length (10 cm).
Step 2: The lens acts as a magnifying glass.
Step 3: Image is virtual, upright, magnified.
Answer: Virtual, upright, magnified (magnifying glass).

cards.title: Lenses — Converging and Diverging — Worked Example
points: Example: What type of lens is used to correct short sight (myopia)? Explain.
Step 1: Short sight means the eye focuses light in front of the retina.
Step 2: A diverging (concave) lens spreads light before it enters the eye, moving the focus back onto the retina.
Answer: A diverging lens is used to correct myopia.

Gaps allow the bridge to expand in summer without buckling.

cards.title: Kinetic Theory — The Particle Model
points: Explanation: The **kinetic theory of matter** explains the physical properties of solids, liquids, and gases in terms of the motion and arrangement of particles.
More to know: All matter is made of tiny, constantly moving particles. The differences between states arise from the spacing and motion of these particles.

Definition: The **kinetic theory** describes matter as composed of particles in constant motion. The properties of solids, liquids, and gases are explained by the arrangement and movement of these particles.

cards.title: Kinetic Theory — The Particle Model — Worked Example
points: Example: A gas has a volume of 2.0 m³ at a temperature of 300 K. What is its volume at 450 K, if pressure is constant?
Step 1: Charles's Law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ → V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.0 × 450/300 = 3.0 m³
Answer: V₂ = 3.0 m³

cards.title: Kinetic Theory — The Particle Model — Worked Example
points: Example: A gas occupies 3.0 m³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. If the pressure is increased to 150 kPa at constant temperature, what is the new volume?
Step 1: P₁ = 100 kPa
Step 2: P₂ = 150 kPa
Step 3: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 100 × 3.0 / 150 = 2.0 m³
Answer: V₂ = 2.0 m³

cards.title: Kinetic Theory — The Particle Model — Worked Example
points: Example: A gas has a volume of 4.0 m³ at 200 kPa and 400 K. What is its volume at 300 kPa and 600 K?
Step 1: P₁=200 kPa, V₁=4.0 m³, T₁=400 K
Step 2: P₂=300 kPa, T₂=600 K
Step 3: Using P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ → V₂ = P₁V₁T₂/(P₂T₁) = 200×4.0×600/(300×400) = 4.0 m³
Answer: V₂ = 4.0 m³

cards.title: Thermal Properties — Expansion, Thermometers, Heat Capacities
points: Explanation: Thermal properties describe how materials respond to changes in temperature: they expand, change state, and absorb or release heat.
More to know: In this section, we study thermal expansion, thermometers, and the quantitative measurement of heat using specific heat capacity and latent heat.

cards.title: Thermal Properties — Expansion, Thermometers, Heat Capacities — Worked Example
points: Example: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C? (c_water = 4200 J/kg°C)
Answer: Q = 504 kJ

cards.title: Thermal Properties — Expansion, Thermometers, Heat Capacities — Worked Example
points: Example: A 0.5 kg block of ice at 0°C is melted. How much heat is required? (Latent heat of fusion of ice = 334,000 J/kg)
Step 1: l = 334,000 J/kg
Answer: Q = 167 kJ

cards.title: Thermal Properties — Expansion, Thermometers, Heat Capacities — Worked Example
points: Example: A heater supplies 500 J of energy per second. How long will it take to heat 0.2 kg of water from 15°C to 100°C? (c_water = 4200 J/kg°C)
Step 2: Power = 500 W
Step 3: Time = Energy / Power = 71,400 / 500 = 142.8 s ≈ 143 s
Answer: Time ≈ 143 s (2 min 23 s)

cards.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection, Radiation
points: Explanation: Heat can be transferred from one place to another by three mechanisms: **conduction**, **convection**, and **radiation**.
More to know: Each mechanism operates in different media and under different conditions. Understanding them helps explain everyday phenomena and design efficient heating systems.

cards.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection, Radiation — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain why a vacuum flask is able to keep hot liquids hot for a long time.
Step 1: The vacuum between the walls prevents conduction and convection.
Step 2: The silvered surfaces reflect radiation back into the liquid.
Step 3: The stopper and insulating materials reduce heat loss by conduction.
Answer: Vacuum reduces conduction and convection; silvered surfaces reduce radiation.

cards.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection, Radiation — Worked Example
points: Example: Why are car radiators usually painted black?
Step 1: Black surfaces are good emitters of radiation.
Step 2: The radiator needs to lose heat to the surrounding air efficiently.
Step 3: Black colour enhances heat transfer by radiation.
Answer: Black is a good emitter, so heat is lost more rapidly.

cards.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction, Convection, Radiation — Worked Example
points: Example: A solar water heater has a black collector plate. Why is it black?
Step 1: Black surfaces are good absorbers of radiation (sunlight).
Step 2: This maximises the energy absorbed from the sun.
Step 3: The absorbed energy heats the water in the pipes.
Answer: Black absorbs radiation well, increasing the efficiency of heating.

cards.title: Mechanical Waves — Properties and Characteristics
points: Explanation: A **wave** is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Waves are everywhere — in water, sound, light, and even earthquakes.
More to know: In this section, we study the properties of mechanical waves: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, and speed. We also distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves.

Definition: A **mechanical wave** is a disturbance that transfers energy through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas). The particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions, but do not move with the wave.

cards.title: Mechanical Waves — Properties and Characteristics — Worked Example
points: Example: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. Calculate the wave speed.
Answer: v = 100 m/s

cards.title: Mechanical Waves — Properties and Characteristics — Worked Example
points: Example: A sound wave has a speed of 340 m/s and a frequency of 680 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
Answer: λ = 0.5 m

cards.title: Mechanical Waves — Properties and Characteristics — Worked Example
points: Example: A water wave has a wavelength of 1.5 m and a speed of 3 m/s. Calculate its frequency.
Step 1: f = v / λ = 3 / 1.5 = 2 Hz
Answer: f = 2 Hz

cards.title: Mechanical Waves — Properties and Characteristics — Worked Example
points: Example: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency.
Answer: f = 50 Hz

cards.title: Sound — A Longitudinal Wave
points: Explanation: **Sound** is produced by a vibrating object. It is a mechanical, longitudinal wave that travels through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas).
More to know: Sound consists of **compressions** (regions of high pressure where particles are close together) and **rarefactions** (regions of low pressure where particles are spread apart).

cards.title: Sound — A Longitudinal Wave — Worked Example
points: Example: A person shouts near a cliff and hears an echo 1.5 s later. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, calculate the distance to the cliff.
Step 1: Time for echo = 1.5 s
Step 2: Speed = 340 m/s
Step 3: Distance = speed × time / 2 (echo travels there and back)
Answer: Distance = 255 m

cards.title: Sound — A Longitudinal Wave — Worked Example
points: Example: A sound wave has a frequency of 256 Hz and a wavelength of 1.33 m. Calculate the speed of sound.
Answer: v ≈ 340 m/s

cards.title: Sound — A Longitudinal Wave — Worked Example
points: Example: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Step 1: Sound is a mechanical wave — it needs particles to vibrate and transfer energy.
Step 2: A vacuum contains no particles (no medium).
Step 3: Without particles, there is nothing to carry the sound wave.
Answer: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to vibrate and transfer the wave.

cards.title: Electromagnetic Waves — The Spectrum
points: Explanation: **Electromagnetic (EM) waves** are transverse waves that consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields. Unlike mechanical waves, they do not need a medium to travel through.
More to know: All EM waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s). They differ in wavelength and frequency, which determines their properties and applications.

cards.title: Electromagnetic Waves — The Spectrum — Worked Example
points: Example: An electromagnetic wave has a frequency of 100 MHz. Calculate its wavelength. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Step 1: f = 100 MHz = 100 × 10⁶ Hz = 10⁸ Hz
Step 2: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
Step 3: λ = c / f = 3 × 10⁸ / 10⁸ = 3 m
Answer: λ = 3 m (radio wave)

cards.title: Electromagnetic Waves — The Spectrum — Worked Example
points: Example: Place the following EM waves in order of increasing frequency: X-rays, infrared, microwaves, visible light, gamma rays.
Step 1: Increasing frequency means from longest wavelength to shortest.
Step 2: Order: microwaves → infrared → visible light → X-rays → gamma rays
Answer: Microwaves → Infrared → Visible → X-rays → Gamma rays

snippets: Renewable sources can be replenished naturally; non-renewable sources are finite and will eventually run out.

cards.title: Work Done in Work Energy And Power
points: Explanation: **Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance, in the direction of the force.** If you push a wall and it does not move, you have used force, but you have done no work — because nothing moved.
More to know: The formula for work done is: **W = F × d**, where W is work (in joules, J), F is force (in newtons, N), and d is the distance moved in the direction of the force (in metres, m).
Definition: **Work Done** is the product of force and the distance moved in the direction of that force. W = F × d

cards.title: Work Done — Worked Example
points: Example: A force of 20 N pushes a box 5 m across a floor. Find the work done.
Answer: W = 100 J

cards.title: Work Done — Worked Example
points: Example: A boy lifts a 40 N bag 2 m off the ground. Find the work done.
Answer: W = 80 J

cards.title: Forms & Stores of Energy
points: Explanation: **Energy is the capacity to do work.** It is measured in joules (J), same as work. Energy can be stored in different ways, called energy stores.
More to know: **Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE)** is energy stored in an object because of its height above the ground. GPE = m × g × h (mass × gravity × height).
Definition: **GPE = mgh** (m = mass in kg, g = gravity ≈ 10 m/s², h = height in m) **KE = ½mv²** (m = mass in kg, v = speed in m/s)

cards.title: Forms & Stores of Energy — Worked Example
points: Example: Find the GPE of a 2 kg ball held 5 m above the ground. (g = 10 m/s²)
Step 1: GPE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J
Answer: GPE = 100 J

cards.title: Forms & Stores of Energy — Worked Example
points: Example: Find the KE of a 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s.
Step 1: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 3 × 16 = 24 J
Answer: KE = 24 J

cards.title: The Principle of Conservation of Energy
points: Explanation: **The Law of Conservation of Energy** says energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transformed from one store to another.
More to know: On a roller coaster or a swinging pendulum, as height (and GPE) decreases, speed (and KE) increases. If we ignore friction, the GPE lost equals the KE gained.
Definition: **Conservation of Energy:** Total energy before = Total energy after. Loss in GPE = Gain in KE (no friction)

cards.title: The Principle of Conservation of Energy — Worked Example
points: Example: A 2 kg ball falls from 10 m. Find its speed just before hitting the ground (g = 10 m/s², ignore friction).
Step 1: GPE at top = mgh = 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J
Step 2: GPE lost = KE gained, so KE = 200 J
Answer: v ≈ 14.1 m/s

cards.title: Power and Efficiency
points: Explanation: **Power** is the rate of doing work, or the rate of transferring energy. P = W / t (work done ÷ time taken).
More to know: The unit of power is the **watt (W)**. 1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s).
Definition: **Power: P = W / t** (measured in watts, W) **Efficiency = (Useful output ÷ Total input) × 100%**

cards.title: Power and Efficiency — Worked Example
points: Example: A motor does 600 J of work in 3 s. Find its power.
Answer: P = 200 W

cards.title: Power and Efficiency — Worked Example
points: Example: A machine takes in 500 J and produces 350 J of useful energy. Find its efficiency.
Step 1: Useful output = 350 J
Step 2: Total input = 500 J
Step 3: Efficiency = (350 / 500) × 100 = 70%
Answer: Efficiency = 70%

cards.title: Energy Resources & Worked Examples
points: Explanation: **Renewable energy resources** (solar, wind, hydro) can be replaced naturally and will not run out. **Non-renewable resources** (fossil fuels, nuclear) are limited and will eventually run out.
More to know: Renewable sources are cleaner but often depend on weather. Non-renewable sources give a lot of reliable power but cause pollution and cannot be replaced.

cards.title: Implications in Agriculture
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Farmers face many uncertainties in their operations. Understanding the difference between risk and uncertainty is important for decision‑making.
Fertiliser application: Farmers must apply fertiliser at the optimum rate. Too little reduces yields; too much wastes money and can damage crops.
Labour management: Adding more labour to a fixed piece of land eventually leads to diminishing returns (too many workers may get in each other's way).
Irrigation: Over‑irrigation can lead to waterlogging, salinisation, and reduced yields.
Livestock stocking rates: Adding more animals to a fixed grazing area eventually reduces individual animal growth and may degrade the pasture.

cards.title: Ways of Minimising the Effects of Risk and Uncertainty
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Diversification: Growing different crops and keeping different livestock reduces the impact of failure in one enterprise. Zimbabwe example: A farmer growing both maize and tobacco, and keeping cattle.
Insurance: Crop insurance, livestock insurance, and income insurance can protect against losses. Zimbabwe example: Agricultural insurance through the Agricultural Insurance Company (AIC).
Contract farming: Entering into contracts with buyers (e.g., tobacco companies) guarantees a market and price, reducing price risk.
Use of technology: Improved seeds, irrigation, pest control, and forecasting reduce production risk.
Storage: Storing produce (e.g., in silos) allows farmers to sell when prices are higher, reducing price risk.
Flexible planning: Develop contingency plans for different scenarios (e.g., drought plan, pest outbreak plan).

cards.title: Uncertainty in Agri Business
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Uncertainty occurs when the possible outcomes and their probabilities are unknown or cannot be estimated.
Agricultural examples: Climate change: Future rainfall patterns and temperatures are uncertain – exact probabilities are unknown.
New pests/diseases: A new disease may emerge (e.g., African swine fever) with unknown spread and impact.
Policy changes: Government policies on subsidies, taxes, or trade can change unexpectedly.
Characteristics: Cannot be easily quantified or insured against. Requires flexible strategies.

cards.title: Interpreting the Law from Graphs
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Total Product (TP) curve: The TP curve slopes upward initially (Stage 1), then continues to rise but flattens out (Stage 2), and eventually declines (Stage 3).
Marginal Product (MP) curve: The MP curve rises (Stage 1), then peaks, then declines (Stage 2), and eventually becomes negative (Stage 3).
Average Product (AP) curve: The AP curve rises, peaks, and then declines (but stays positive until Stage 3).
Optimum input level: The point where MP = AP (maximum average product) is the most efficient use of inputs. Beyond this, returns diminish.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details

Production risk: Yields vary due to weather, pests, and diseases. Historical data can estimate the likelihood of different outcomes.
Characteristics: Can be quantified and insured against (e.g., crop insurance).

cards.title: Agri Business: What to Remember
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Law of diminishing returns: Adding more inputs to fixed resources eventually gives smaller extra outputs (fertiliser, labour, irrigation). Farmers must find the optimum input level (where MP = AP).

• Risk vs uncertainty: Risk has measurable probabilities (price, yield); uncertainty has unknown probabilities (climate change, new diseases). Minimise effects through diversification, insurance, contracts, technology, and flexible planning.

• Decision‑making: Steps include identify problem, gather information, identify alternatives, analyse, choose, implement, monitor. Economic factors influencing decisions: input/output prices, labour costs, policies, interest rates, and markets.

• Marketing legislation: Laws regulate the sale of agricultural products. In Zimbabwe, controlled products include grains (GMB), tobacco (TIMB/TAF), cotton (COTCO), sugar (SMC), dairy (ZDIT), meat, and horticulture (HEA). Legislation protects farmers and ensures quality.

cards.title: Stages of the Law of Diminishing Returns
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Stage 1 – Increasing returns (positive returns): As more input is added, total output increases at an increasing rate. This is because fixed resources are being used more efficiently. Example: Adding fertiliser to a field for the first time – yields increase significantly.

Stage 2 – Diminishing returns: As more input is added, total output increases but at a decreasing rate. This is the most common stage in agriculture. Example: Adding more fertiliser to a field – yields still increase, but each additional unit of fertiliser gives a smaller increase in yield.

Stage 3 – Negative returns: Adding more input actually reduces total output. This is due to overcrowding, toxicity, or other negative effects. Example: Excessive fertiliser application burns crops and reduces yields.

snippets: Definition: The male reproductive system produces sperm and delivers it to the female for fertilisation. In ruminants, the male is called a bull (cattle), ram (sheep), or buck (goat).

Definition: The female reproductive system produces eggs (ova), supports fertilisation, and nurtures the developing foetus until birth. In ruminants, the female is called a cow (cattle), ewe (sheep), or doe (goat).
Definition: A balanced ration provides all the nutrients an animal needs for maintenance (staying alive and healthy) and production (growth, milk, meat, wool, or reproduction).
The Pearson Square is a simple method for calculating the proportions of two feeds needed to achieve a desired nutrient level (usually protein or energy).

cards.title: Pearson Square Method
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The Pearson Square is a simple method for calculating the proportions of two feeds needed to achieve a desired nutrient level (usually protein or energy).
Problem: You need to formulate a ration with 14% crude protein (CP) for growing sheep using maize meal (9% CP) and cottonseed cake (38% CP).
Step 1: Draw a square and put the desired protein (14%) in the centre.
Step 2: Put the protein of each feed in the left corners.
Step 3: Subtract diagonally (use positive numbers): 38 – 14 = 24 parts maize meal 14 – 9 = 5 parts cottonseed cake
Step 4: Total parts = 24 + 5 = 29
Step 5: Percentage of each feed: Maize meal: (24 ÷ 29) × 100 = 82.8% Cottonseed cake: (5 ÷ 29) × 100 = 17.2%

cards.title: External Parasites (Ectoparasites)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The Animal Health Act is the legislation in Zimbabwe that governs the prevention, control, and eradication of animal diseases. It provides the legal framework for animal health management.
Types: Ticks: e.g., Amblyomma (bont tick), Rhipicephalus (brown tick). Transmit diseases like East Coast Fever (ECF) and anaplasmosis.
Mites: Cause mange (skin irritation, hair loss).
Lice: Cause irritation, biting, and anaemia.
Flies: e.g., blowflies (myiasis – maggots in wounds), stable flies.
Life cycle: Adult ticks/mites/lice reproduce on the animal, lay eggs, and larvae develop on the animal or in the environment.
Symptoms: Irritation, scratching, hair loss, skin lesions, anaemia, weight loss, reduced production, and transmission of diseases.

cards.title: Eggs (Layers) in Animal Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Collection: Collect eggs at least twice daily to prevent breakage and soiling.
Cleaning: Wipe clean (do not wash) to remove dirt. Washing removes the protective bloom and reduces shelf life.
Grading: Sort by size (small, medium, large, extra large) and quality (cracked, dirty, stained).
Packaging: Use clean, sturdy cartons (egg trays) to reduce breakage.
Storage: Store at 4–10°C (refrigerated) to maintain freshness.
Marketing: Sell to households, restaurants, supermarkets, or baking companies.

Breeding: Use controlled breeding to improve genetics. Match bulls/rams/bucks to females. Keep breeding records.

Health: Vaccinate against common diseases (FMD, anthrax). Control parasites (dipping, deworming). Monitor for signs of illness.

cards.title: Cross‑breeding in Animal Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Mating animals of different breeds.
Advantages: Heterosis (hybrid vigour): Offspring are stronger, more productive, and more disease‑resistant than either parent.
Combines desirable traits from different breeds.
Disadvantages: Offspring may not breed true (traits vary).
Requires careful selection of parent breeds.
Zimbabwe example: Brahman (heat‑tolerant) × Hereford (good beef) for beef production in the Lowveld.

Reproductive traits: Fertility, litter size, ease of calving/lambing/kidding.

Conformation: Physical structure (legs, udder, body shape) that affects performance and longevity.

Record keeping: Keep detailed records of all animals (birth, parentage, health, production) to make informed selection decisions.

cards.title: Artificial Selection in Animal Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The process by which humans select animals with desirable traits for breeding, rather than allowing natural selection to occur.
Methods: Phenotypic selection: Select animals based on their physical appearance (size, conformation, milk yield).
Pedigree selection: Select animals based on the performance of their ancestors.
Progeny testing: Select animals based on the performance of their offspring.
Performance testing: Select animals based on their own performance (e.g., growth rate, milk production).

cards.title: Internal Parasites (Endoparasites)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Types: Roundworms (nematodes): e.g., Haemonchus (barber's pole worm), Ostertagia.
Life cycle: Eggs passed in faeces → larvae develop on pasture → ingested by animal → larvae mature in the gut/liver → produce eggs → cycle repeats.
Symptoms: Weight loss, diarrhoea, anaemia (pale mucous membranes), rough coat, reduced production, bottle jaw (swelling under jaw), death.

Prevention and treatment: Prevention: Rotate pastures, maintain good hygiene, practice clean grazing (defer grazing on contaminated pastures). Treatment: Deworming with anthelmintics (e.g., ivermectin, albendazole).

Definition: Respiration and photosynthesis are two fundamental processes in plants. Photosynthesis produces food (glucose) using sunlight, while respiration breaks down food to release energy.

cards.title: Precautions When Storing Agrochemicals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Toxicity is the degree to which a chemical can harm living organisms. Agrochemicals are classified by their toxicity to humans, animals, and the environment.
Storage area: Store agrochemicals in a dedicated, well-ventilated, lockable store away from food, feed, and water sources.
Container integrity: Keep agrochemicals in their original containers with intact labels. Check for leaks and damage regularly.
Temperature and light: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and extreme temperatures (some chemicals can degrade or become volatile).
Inventory: Keep an inventory of stored agrochemicals and use older stock first (FIFO – First In, First Out).
Spill containment: Have spill containment materials (sand, sawdust, absorbent pads) and a spill response plan.
Disposal: Dispose of empty containers and unused chemicals safely (e.g., triple-rinse containers and return to collection points; never burn or bury).

cards.title: General Formula in Crop Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: A knapsack sprayer is a hand-operated or motorised sprayer worn on the back (like a backpack). It is commonly used for applying pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides on small to medium-sized farms.
Amount of chemical = (Rate per hectare × Area) / (Volume per hectare ÷ Tank capacity)

Example for a knapsack sprayer (15-litre tank): If the spray volume is 200 L/ha, one knapsack covers 15/200 = 0.075 ha. If the herbicide rate is 2 L/ha, you need 2 × 0.075 = 0.15 litres (150 ml) of herbicide per knapsack.
Tank: Description: The container that holds the spray solution (water + chemical). Usually made of plastic or metal, with a capacity of 10-20 litres. Function: Stores the liquid to be sprayed.
Pump: Description: A hand-operated or motorised pump that pressurises the liquid in the tank. Function: Creates the pressure needed to spray the liquid.

Lance (spray wand): Description: A long, tubular rod attached to the tank with a hose. It has a trigger and a nozzle at the end. Function: Allows the operator to direct the spray to the target plants.

Nozzle: Description: The tip at the end of the lance that controls the spray pattern and droplet size. Function: Atomises the liquid into droplets for even coverage. Different nozzles give different spray patterns (e.g., fan nozzle, cone nozzle, hollow cone).

cards.title: Importance of Respiration
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: While aerobic respiration requires oxygen, anaerobic respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen. Both processes release energy from glucose, but they differ in efficiency and products.
Energy production: Respiration releases energy (ATP) that powers all life processes – growth, reproduction, transport of nutrients, and movement.
Growth and development: The energy from respiration is used for cell division, elongation, and differentiation.
Transport: Energy is needed for active transport of minerals and water.
Repair and maintenance: Energy is required to repair damaged tissues and maintain cellular functions.

cards.title: Understanding LD50 in Crop Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Calculating chemical mixing ratios involves determining the correct amount of chemical to mix with water to achieve the recommended concentration for spraying.
LD50: Lethal Dose that kills 50% of a test population. It is measured in mg of chemical per kg of body weight.
Lower LD50 = higher toxicity. A chemical with an LD50 of 5 mg/kg is much more toxic than one with an LD50 of 500 mg/kg.
Importance: LD50 values help farmers and regulators understand the risk of a chemical and determine appropriate safety measures.

cards.title: Significance in Crop Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Respiration and photosynthesis are two fundamental processes in plants. Photosynthesis produces food (glucose) using sunlight, while respiration breaks down food to release energy.
Aerobic respiration: Highly efficient, produces large amounts of energy for active growth and development.
Anaerobic respiration: Less efficient but allows plants to survive in oxygen-poor conditions (e.g., waterlogged soils). However, ethanol production can be toxic to plants over time.

cards.title: Precautions When Using Agrochemicals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Personal protective equipment (PPE): Wear protective clothing: gloves, boots, overalls, goggles, and a mask or respirator. This prevents skin contact and inhalation of toxic substances.
Read the label: Always read the product label and follow the manufacturer's instructions. The label provides information on dosage, application method, safety precautions, and first aid.
Calibration: Calibrate sprayers correctly to ensure the correct application rate. Over-application can damage crops and harm the environment; under-application may not control the pest.
Avoid contamination: Do not eat, drink, or smoke while handling agrochemicals. Wash hands and exposed skin thoroughly after handling.
Spraying conditions: Avoid spraying on windy days (to prevent drift) or before rain (to prevent runoff). Spray early morning or late afternoon to avoid high temperatures and direct sunlight.
Clean equipment: Clean sprayers and equipment thoroughly after use to prevent contamination and blockages.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Aerobic Respiration: Glucose + Oxygen → CO₂ + Water + Energy (ATP). Occurs in mitochondria. Provides energy for growth, transport, and all life processes.

• Respiration vs Photosynthesis: Photosynthesis produces glucose (stores energy); respiration breaks it down (releases energy). They are complementary processes.
• Plant Tropisms: Phototropism (light), Thigmotropism (touch), Gravitropism (gravity), Hydrotropism (water) – directional growth responses that help plants survive and thrive.
• Agrochemical Safety: Wear PPE, read labels, calibrate, store safely, and dispose of containers correctly. Toxicity is classified by WHO (I-IV) based on LD50 values.
• Sprayer Parts: Knapsack sprayer has a tank, pump, lance, nozzle, hose, strainer, pressure regulator, and harness. Correct mixing calculations are essential for effective and safe application.

cards.title: Phototropism (Response to Light)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Growth of a plant in response to light.
Direction: Positive phototropism: Growing towards light (e.g., shoots and leaves). This maximises light absorption for photosynthesis.
Negative phototropism: Growing away from light (e.g., roots). Roots grow away from light to seek moisture and nutrients in the soil.
Importance: Ensures plants get maximum light for photosynthesis, which is essential for food production.
Example: A houseplant bends towards a window to capture more sunlight.

cards.title: Gravitropism (Response to Gravity)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Growth of a plant in response to gravity.
Direction: Positive gravitropism: Growing towards gravity (e.g., roots). Roots grow downwards into the soil to anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals.
Negative gravitropism: Growing away from gravity (e.g., shoots). Shoots grow upwards towards light and air.
Importance: Ensures roots grow into the soil for anchorage and absorption, and shoots grow upwards for light exposure.
Example: A seed planted upside down will still send roots downwards and shoots upwards.

cards.title: Thigmotropism (Response to Touch)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Growth of a plant in response to touch or physical contact.
Direction: Positive thigmotropism – growing towards or around an object (e.g., climbing plants).
Importance: Allows climbing plants to attach to supports (trees, walls, trellises), helping them reach sunlight and support their growth.
Example: Bean plants curl around a trellis; tendrils of grapes and passion fruit wrap around supports.

cards.title: Steps for Calculating Mixing Ratios
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Step 1: Read the label. The label will specify the recommended dosage (e.g., 2 litres per hectare, or 50 ml per 20 litres of water).

Step 2: Calculate the spray volume needed. Determine the area to be sprayed (hectares) and the spray volume required (litres per hectare). For a knapsack sprayer, typical spray volume is 200-400 litres per hectare.
Step 3: Calculate the amount of chemical needed. Amount of chemical = Recommended rate × Area to be sprayed ÷ Concentration of spray solution.
Step 4: Mix carefully. Add water to the sprayer, then add the chemical, then top up with more water. Agitate to mix thoroughly.

cards.title: Example Calculation in Crop Husbandry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Scenario: You need to spray a 1-hectare field with a herbicide. The label says: "Apply 2 litres of product per hectare in 200 litres of water."
Calculation: You need 2 litres of herbicide for 1 hectare.
You need 200 litres of water to mix with the herbicide.
For a smaller area (e.g., 0.5 hectare), you would need: 2 litres × 0.5 = 1 litre of herbicide, and 200 litres × 0.5 = 100 litres of water.

snippets: Definition: An anchor (also called a stay or brace) is a structure used to support and stabilise fence posts, especially at corners, gateways, and changes in direction. Anchors prevent fence posts from leaning or being pulled out of the ground by the tension of the wire.

Definition: To construct a fence, you need to calculate the quantities of materials required (posts, wire, anchors, strainers, and fasteners) based on the length of the fence line and the spacing of materials.
Definition: Anchor construction involves building the support structures that hold fence posts in place, especially at corners, gateways, and changes in direction.
Definition: Livestock buildings are structures designed to house animals (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry). Proper design ensures animal welfare, productivity, and efficient management.

cards.title: Farm Buildings in Farm Structures And Machinery
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Farm roads are essential for accessing fields, moving produce, and transporting inputs. The choice of materials affects the durability and cost of the road.
Definition: Farm road construction involves several steps to ensure the road is durable, well-drained, and suitable for farm vehicles.
Definition: Regular maintenance is essential to keep farm roads in good condition and prevent deterioration.
Costs: materials + labour + transport + contingency

cards.title: Steps for Material Calculation
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Step 1: Measure the perimeter. Measure the total length of the fence line (in metres).
Step 2: Determine post spacing. Decide on the spacing between posts (e.g., 3-5m for intermediate posts, 1-2m for droppers).
Step 3: Calculate the number of posts. Number of posts = (Perimeter ÷ Spacing) + 1 (for the starting post).
Step 4: Determine number of strands. Decide on the number of wire strands (e.g., 4-6 for cattle, 6-8 for sheep/goats).
Step 5: Calculate wire length. Wire length = Perimeter × Number of strands + 10% for wastage and overlaps.
Step 6: Calculate strainers and anchors. Allow for strainer posts at corners and every 100-200m. Allow for anchors at corners and gateways.

cards.title: Steps for Cost Calculation
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Step 1: List all materials. Identify all materials needed: timber, metal sheets, concrete, bricks, nails, cement, etc.
Step 2: Quantify materials. Calculate the quantity of each material needed (e.g., number of sheets, bags of cement, lengths of timber).
Step 3: Estimate material costs. Multiply the quantity by the unit price (e.g., cost per bag, per sheet, per metre).
Step 4: Estimate labour costs. Calculate the number of labour hours or days required and the wage rate.
Step 5: Add other costs. Include transport costs, equipment rental, and contingency (10-15% for unexpected expenses).
Step 6: Calculate total cost. Total cost = Material costs + Labour costs + Other costs + Contingency.

cards.title: Maize Sheller in Farm Structures And Machinery
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Hopper: Description: A funnel-shaped opening at the top where maize cobs are fed into the machine. Function: Guides the cobs into the shelling chamber.
Shelling drum (cylinder): Description: A rotating cylinder with projections (teeth, bars, or spikes) that strike the cobs. Function: Removes the kernels from the cob by impact and friction.
Concave (grating): Description: A curved metal plate with holes or openings that surrounds the shelling drum. Function: Allows kernels to pass through while retaining the cobs.
Screen (sieves): Description: A mesh or perforated plate that separates kernels from broken cobs and chaff. Function: Sorts the shelled grain from the waste.
Fan (blower): Description: A fan that blows air through the machine. Function: Removes chaff and dust from the kernels.
Power source: Description: The motor (electric, petrol, or diesel) or hand crank that drives the machine. Function: Provides the mechanical power for shelling.

cards.title: Maize Sheller – How It Works
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Principle: Impact and friction remove kernels from the cob.
Operation: Feeding: Cobs are fed into the hopper by hand.
Shelling: The shelling drum rotates and strikes the cobs, knocking the kernels off the cob. The concave provides friction to help separate kernels.
Separation: Kernels fall through the holes in the concave and onto the screen. The cob pieces are retained and exit through the waste outlet.
Cleaning: The fan blows air through the machine, removing chaff and dust from the kernels.
Collection: Clean kernels exit through the grain outlet and are collected in bags or containers.

cards.title: Groundnut Sheller – How It Works
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Principle: Friction and pressure crack the shells without damaging the nuts.
Operation: Feeding: Groundnuts are fed into the hopper.
Shelling: The shelling drum with ribs rotates against the concave, cracking the shells through friction and pressure.
Separation: Nuts fall through the screen (mesh) while shell pieces are separated. The screen size can be adjusted to suit different groundnut varieties.
Cleaning: The fan blows away light shell pieces and dust.
Collection: Shelled nuts exit through the nut outlet and are collected.

cards.title: Steps for Constructing a Deadman Anchor
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Step 1: Dig a hole behind the corner post (about 1-1.5m from the post, 0.5-1m deep).
Step 2: Place a log, concrete block, or large stone in the hole.
Step 3: Attach a wire or chain from the deadman to the corner post (at the point where the wire pulls).
Step 4: Backfill the hole with soil and compact well to secure the deadman.
Step 5: Tension the wire between the post and the deadman to make it tight.

cards.title: Steps for Constructing a Strainer Post Anchor
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Step 1: Dig a hole for the strainer post (about 1-1.2m deep).
Step 2: Place the strainer post in the hole and backfill with soil, compacting well.
Step 3: Place a brace (a diagonal strut) from the strainer post to a secondary post (blocking post) set about 2-3m away.
Step 4: Secure the brace with nails or wire.
Step 5: Tension the wire from the strainer post using a wire strainer.

cards.title: Voluntary Organisations in General Agriculture
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: International conventions are agreements between countries to cooperate on specific issues, including wildlife conservation.
Zimbabwe Conservation Taskforce (ZCT): Role: Monitors wildlife and conservation issues, raises awareness, and advocates for wildlife protection.
African Wildlife Foundation (AWF): Role: Works to conserve wildlife and ecosystems in Africa, including programmes in Zimbabwe.
International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN): Role: Provides global conservation guidance, assesses species status (Red List), and promotes sustainable use.

Local conservation organisations: Examples: Save Valley Conservancy, Matopos Rhino Conservation, Zimbabwe Elephant Conservation Trust. Role: Work on specific conservation issues (elephants, rhinos, protected areas).

Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD): Purpose: To conserve biological diversity, promote sustainable use, and ensure fair sharing of benefits. Zimbabwe's role: Zimbabwe is a signatory and has developed a National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP).

Ramsar Convention (Wetlands): Purpose: To conserve wetlands and their resources (waterfowl habitat). Zimbabwe's role: Zimbabwe has designated several Ramsar sites, including Mana Pools, Lake Chivero, and Monavale Vlei.

cards.title: Floods in General Agriculture
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: An overflow of water that submerges land.
Effects: Crop loss: Crops are drowned and die. Floodwaters can wash away soil and seeds.
Soil erosion: Floodwater washes away fertile topsoil.
Infrastructure damage: Roads, bridges, and irrigation systems are damaged.
Livestock losses: Animals may drown or be washed away.
Zimbabwe examples: Floods occur in the Lowveld (Save, Runde, and Limpopo river basins) and along the Zambezi River. Cyclone Idai (2019) caused severe flooding in Chimanimani and Chipinge districts.

Loss of pastures: Grazing land is destroyed.
Loss of livestock: Animals may be killed or injured.
Soil degradation: Organic matter is burned, reducing soil fertility and increasing erosion.
Loss of biodiversity: Wildlife and habitats are destroyed.

cards.title: Hailstorm in General Agriculture
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: A storm with falling hail (balls of ice) that can damage crops.
Effects: Physical damage: Hailstones bruise, shred, and destroy leaves, stems, and fruits. Can completely destroy a crop.
Reduced yields: Damaged plants may not recover, leading to significant yield losses.
Secondary infections: Damaged tissues are susceptible to diseases.
Zimbabwe examples: Hailstorms occur in the Eastern Highlands and parts of Mashonaland, particularly during summer storms. Tobacco and horticultural crops (vegetables, fruits) are most at risk.

cards.title: Cyclones in General Agriculture
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Large storm systems with strong winds and heavy rainfall.
Effects: Wind damage: Strong winds flatten crops (lodging), break trees, and destroy buildings.
Infrastructure damage: Roads, bridges, and irrigation systems are destroyed.
Loss of life: Cyclones can cause fatalities.
Zimbabwe examples: Cyclone Idai (2019) and Cyclone Eline (2000) affected Zimbabwe, causing widespread damage in the Eastern Highlands and parts of Manicaland.

cards.title: Stages of the Nitrogen Cycle
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Nitrogen fixation: Atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) is converted into ammonia (NH₃) or nitrate (NO₃⁻) by: Biological fixation: Bacteria like Rhizobium (in root nodules of legumes) and free‑living bacteria (e.g., Azotobacter ).
Industrial fixation: The Haber‑Bosch process (manufacture of fertilisers).
Atmospheric fixation: Lightning converts N₂ to nitrate.
Nitrogen assimilation: Plants absorb ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) from the soil and use them to make amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Ammonification (mineralisation): Decomposition of organic matter (dead plants, animals, manure) by bacteria and fungi releases ammonium (NH₄⁺) back into the soil.
Nitrification: Conversion of ammonium (NH₄⁺) to nitrite (NO₂⁻) by bacteria like Nitrosomonas, and then to nitrate (NO₃⁻) by Nitrobacter. Nitrate is the form most readily taken up by plants.

cards.title: Drip Irrigation Components
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Drip line (drip tube): Structure: Thin plastic tube with emitters (drippers) at regular intervals. Function: Delivers water directly to the plant root zone at a slow, steady rate.
Emitter (dripper): Structure: Small device that regulates water flow (usually 2–8 L/hour). Function: Releases water drop by drop.
Filter: Structure: Mesh or disc filter. Function: Removes particles to prevent clogging of emitters.
Pressure regulator: Structure: Valve that maintains constant pressure. Function: Ensures uniform water delivery across the system.

cards.title: Pumps in Soil And Water
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Centrifugal pump: Structure: An impeller (rotating disc) inside a casing that spins water outward by centrifugal force. Function: Lifts water from a source (river, dam, borehole) and pushes it through pipes to the field.
Submersible pump: Structure: A sealed motor and pump unit that operates underwater. Function: Pumps water from deep boreholes or wells.
Treadle pump: Structure: A foot‑operated piston pump. Function: Used by small‑scale farmers to draw water from shallow wells or streams.

cards.title: Sprinkler Systems in Soil And Water

o-level/form-4/combined-science/Learning.title: Biology: Ecology, Nutrition, Respiration, Transport, Reproduction & Health
snippets: Ecology is the study of how living things interact with one another and with the non-living things around them. Nothing in nature lives alone: a maize plant needs sunlight, water and soil minerals; a locust needs the maize plant; a lizard needs the locust. Ecology is simply the science of following those connections and working out what happens when one of them is broken.

Before you can answer any ecology question you must be comfortable with five words that examiners use constantly. They describe the same piece of nature at bigger and bigger scales, so learn them as a ladder, from smallest to largest.
Every ecosystem is built from two kinds of components. If a question asks you to “describe the components of an ecosystem”, you must give examples from both halves to get full marks.
The living things in an ecosystem are grouped by how they get their food, not by how big they are.

cards.title: Quick self-test in Biology: Ecology, Nutrition, Respiration, Transport, Reproduction & Health
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Every living cell needs energy all the time — to build new molecules, to move substances across membranes, to contract muscles, to send nerve impulses and to keep warm. That energy is locked up inside glucose, and the process that releases it is called respiration.

Definition: Respiration is not breathing. Breathing (properly called ventilation ) is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens inside cells. A person under anaesthetic can be ventilated by a machine, but it is still their own cells that respire. Earthworms and plants respire without having lungs at all.
Explanation: Word equation: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy

cards.title: Must-know definitions in Biology: Ecology, Nutrition, Respiration, Transport, Reproduction & Health
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Ecology, ecosystem, habitat, population, community, producer, consumer, decomposer, food chain, food web, trophic level, biomass, biodiversity, eutrophication.

Definition: Nutrition is the way an organism takes in and uses food. Food does three jobs in the body: it supplies energy for every activity from breathing to running, it supplies materials for growth and repair of cells and tissues, and it supplies substances that protect us from disease. If any one of these is missing the body cannot work properly, no matter how full the stomach feels.

Definition: This is why a person can eat a large plate of sadza every day and still be malnourished. Sadza is almost pure carbohydrate: it fills the stomach and gives energy, but on its own it gives almost no protein, no vitamins and very little mineral content. What the body needs is a balanced diet.
Growing children and teenagers need extra protein and calcium for new tissue and bones.
Pregnant women need extra protein, iron, calcium and folic acid for the developing baby.
Breastfeeding mothers need extra energy, protein, calcium and fluids to produce milk.
People doing heavy manual work (farming, mining, construction) need much more energy than people who sit at a desk.
Elderly people need less energy but still need protein, calcium and vitamins.

cards.title: Diagram practice in Biology: Ecology, Nutrition, Respiration, Transport, Reproduction & Health
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Be able to draw and label from memory: a potometer, a cross-section through artery, vein and capillary, and the human heart showing all four chambers, the four main vessels and the direction of blood flow.

Definition: Reproduction is the process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. It is the only one of the seven life processes that an individual can live without — but without it a species would disappear in a single generation.
Explanation: These are methods farmers and gardeners use to multiply plants deliberately, because they produce offspring identical to a parent with desirable qualities.
Cuttings: a piece of stem with a few buds is cut off, often dipped in rooting hormone, and planted. Used for cassava, sugar cane, roses and hibiscus.
Layering: a low branch is bent down and part of it buried while still attached to the parent. Once roots have formed the branch is cut off. Used for jasmine and raspberries.

Grafting: a shoot (the scion ) from a plant with good fruit is joined onto the rooted stem (the stock ) of a hardy plant, and the join is bound until the tissues unite. Used widely on citrus, mango, avocado and grapes.
Budding: a single bud, rather than a whole shoot, is slipped under the bark of the stock. Common for roses and citrus.
Tissue culture: tiny pieces of plant tissue are grown on sterile nutrient jelly in a laboratory to produce thousands of identical, disease-free plants.

cards.title: Careful with the words
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Stem tuber (potato) is a swollen stem; root tuber (sweet potato, cassava) is a swollen root. Grafting uses a scion joined to a stock. Contraception prevents pregnancy — it is not the same as preventing infection.

Explanation: We are surrounded by pathogens — micro-organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa that cause disease. The reason we are not permanently ill is that the body has an impressive set of defences, from the physical barrier of the skin right through to specially trained white blood cells that remember an invader for life.
Explanation: First line — keeping pathogens out
Skin — a tough, dry, unbroken barrier that most pathogens cannot cross.
Mucus and cilia in the nose and airways — trap dust and germs, then sweep them away from the lungs.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach — kills most bacteria swallowed with food.
Tears and saliva — contain the enzyme lysozyme, which destroys bacterial cell walls.
Blood clotting — quickly seals cuts so germs cannot get in.

cards.title: Experiment 1: Estimating a Plant Population Using Quadrats
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To estimate the number of a particular plant (for example blackjack) growing in a large field, without having to count every single one.
Explanation: Materials: A 1 m × 1 m quadrat frame, two long tape measures, a random number table or calculator, pegs, a notebook and pen.
Explanation: Specimen results: Counts of 4, 6, 3, 5, 7, 5, 4, 6, 8 and 2 plants give a total of 50 plants in 10 m², so the mean is 5 plants per m².
The atom starts as part of a carbon dioxide molecule in the air.
A green plant absorbs it and, by photosynthesis, builds it into glucose and then into starch, cellulose and protein. The carbon is now locked inside the plant.
An animal eats the plant, so the carbon becomes part of the animal.
The plant or animal respires, breaking glucose down again and breathing the carbon out as carbon dioxide. The atom is back in the air.
If instead the organism dies, decomposers feed on the remains and release the carbon dioxide as they respire.

cards.title: Experiment 4: Showing that Respiration Releases Heat
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To show that germinating seeds release heat energy as they respire.
Explanation: Materials: Two vacuum (thermos) flasks, two thermometers, germinating seeds, an equal mass of boiled and disinfected seeds, cotton wool.
Explanation: Results: The temperature in flask A (living seeds) rises, often by several degrees. The temperature in flask B (dead seeds) stays about the same.
Baking: yeast in the dough produces carbon dioxide bubbles that make the bread rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.
Brewing: yeast converts the sugars in grain or fruit into ethanol, which is what makes beer and traditional brews alcoholic.
Biogas: anaerobic bacteria break down animal dung in a digester, producing methane that can be burnt for cooking and lighting.
Silage and sour milk: anaerobic bacteria produce lactic acid, which preserves the food by making it too acidic for spoilage organisms.

Explanation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy

Explanation: Large organisms have a problem: the cells deep inside the body are a long way from the food and oxygen they need, and a long way from anywhere to dump their waste. Diffusion alone is far too slow over those distances. Both plants and animals therefore have transport systems — plants move water and food in xylem and phloem, while animals pump blood through a system of vessels.
It pulls water up from the roots to every leaf.
It carries dissolved mineral salts up with that water.
Evaporation cools the leaf on a hot day, just as sweating cools us.
It keeps cells turgid (firm and full of water), which supports soft green stems and keeps leaves spread out to catch light.
It supplies the water needed as a raw material for photosynthesis.

cards.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Drawing food chain arrows the wrong way. The arrow means “is eaten by” and points the way the energy travels.
Saying that energy is recycled. Energy flows one way and is lost as heat; only matter (carbon, nitrogen) is recycled.
Confusing respiration (a chemical reaction in every cell) with breathing (moving air in and out of the lungs).
Writing that plants only respire at night. Plants respire all the time; they only photosynthesise in the light.
Mixing up kwashiorkor (swollen, protein missing) with marasmus (wasted, everything missing).
Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary artery does not.

cards.title: Biology: Ecology, Nutrition, Respiration, Transport, Reproduction & Health: What to Remember
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Ecology: ecosystems have biotic and abiotic components; energy flows one way and about 90% is lost at each trophic level, while carbon and nitrogen are recycled by bacteria and fungi.
• Nutrition: a balanced diet needs all seven nutrient classes; missing one causes a specific deficiency disease, and four simple colour tests identify starch, sugar, protein and fat.
• Respiration: aerobic respiration in mitochondria releases far more energy than anaerobic respiration; anaerobic respiration gives ethanol in yeast and lactic acid in muscle, causing an oxygen debt.
• Transport: transpiration pulls water up the xylem, while blood carries oxygen, food and waste through arteries, capillaries and veins driven by a four-chambered heart.

• Reproduction: vegetative propagation makes clones quickly but with no variation; the human systems produce gametes that fuse in the oviduct, and contraception works by blocking one step in that pathway.
• Health: immunity may be active or passive, natural or artificial; vaccines create memory cells, while HIV destroys the very white blood cells the immune system depends on.

o-level/form-4/combined-science/Learning.title: Chromatography, Periodic Trends, Metals, Titration, Industry & Organic
snippets: A green felt-tip pen looks like it contains one colour. Put a spot of its ink on wet filter paper, though, and the spot spreads out into a blue band and a yellow band. The “green” ink was never one substance at all — it was a mixture of two dyes. The technique that reveals this is called paper chromatography, and it is one of the most useful separation methods in chemistry because it works on extremely small samples.
Two things are happening at the same time, and the balance between them decides how far each substance travels.

A substance that dissolves very well in the solvent and is only weakly attracted to the paper gets carried a long way up. A substance that dissolves poorly and clings tightly to the paper hardly moves at all. Because every substance has its own particular balance of solubility and attraction, each one ends up at a different height — and the mixture has separated itself.
Aim: To find out how many different coloured dyes are present in a sample of black ink.

cards.title: Experiment 5: Titrating Hydrochloric Acid Against Sodium Hydroxide
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To find the volume of hydrochloric acid needed to exactly neutralise 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution.

Explanation: Materials: Burette, clamp and stand, 25 cm³ pipette and filler, conical flask, white tile, funnel, hydrochloric acid of known concentration, sodium hydroxide solution, phenolphthalein indicator, wash bottle of distilled water, eye protection.
Explanation: Average titre: the rough result is always left out of the average. Using the three concordant titres: (23.60 + 23.55 + 23.55) ÷ 3 = 23.57 cm³.
Titrate as usual with indicator, and note the exact titre.
Throw that mixture away and repeat with fresh solutions, adding exactly the same volume of acid but with no indicator, so that the salt solution is not contaminated by the dye.
Pour the neutral solution into an evaporating basin and heat gently until about half the water has evaporated and crystals begin to form at the edges.
Leave the concentrated solution to cool and crystallise slowly. Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals.
Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers or in a warm oven.

Industrial chemistry has a different aim: making the largest amount of product at the lowest cost, safely and as quickly as possible. This is why industrial conditions are always a compromise — a temperature that gives the fastest useful rate rather than the highest yield, and a pressure high enough to help but low enough to afford.

cards.title: Experiment 3: Comparing How Metals React with Dilute Acid
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To place magnesium, zinc, iron and copper in order of reactivity by comparing how fast each reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.
Explanation: Materials: Four test tubes and a rack, dilute hydrochloric acid, equal-sized pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper, a stopwatch, wooden splints, measuring cylinder, eye protection.

Definition: Results: Magnesium fizzes rapidly and the tube gets warm; zinc fizzes steadily; iron gives only slow bubbles; copper shows no reaction at all. The gas gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, which is the test for hydrogen.

points: Explanation: Hydrogen — squeaky pop with a lighted splint · Oxygen — relights a glowing splint · Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky · Ammonia — turns damp red litmus blue.

Definition: Mixing an acid and an alkali is easy. Mixing exactly the right amounts, so that neither is left over, is not — and it matters, because a leftover acid or alkali would contaminate the salt you are trying to make and would make any concentration calculation wrong. Titration is the careful technique that finds that exact point.

Explanation: Universal indicator is not used in titrations. It changes through a whole range of colours gradually, so you cannot pick out one sharp end point. Use methyl orange or phenolphthalein instead.

cards.title: The word “compromise”
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: If a question asks why 450 °C is used in the Haber or Contact process, the answer must contain the idea of a compromise: a lower temperature gives a better yield but is too slow; a higher temperature is fast but the yield falls.

Definition: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of compounds built around chains and rings of carbon atoms. Carbon is unusual because each of its atoms can form four strong bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms, so it can build molecules of almost unlimited length and variety — which is why there are millions of organic compounds but only about a hundred thousand inorganic ones.
Definition: The alcohols are the homologous series whose functional group is the hydroxyl group, –OH. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, and their names all end in -ol.

cards.title: Experiment 1: Separating the Dyes in Black Ink
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To find out how many different coloured dyes are present in a sample of black ink.

Explanation: Materials: Chromatography (or filter) paper, a beaker, a watch glass or lid, a pencil, a ruler, a capillary tube or fine dropper, the ink sample, a suitable solvent (water for water-soluble inks, ethanol for permanent inks), a glass rod or paper clip to suspend the paper.
Explanation: Results: The single black spot separates into several coloured spots at different heights. Each spot is one dye.
One spot from a sample means the sample is a pure substance.
Two or more spots means it is a mixture, and the number of spots is the minimum number of substances present.
To identify what a mixture contains, run known reference substances on the same paper at the same time. Any spot in the mixture that lines up at the same height as a reference spot is that substance.
Some substances are colourless. They are made visible by spraying with a locating agent (such as ninhydrin for amino acids) or by viewing the paper under an ultraviolet lamp.
Food industry: checking which colourings and additives are in a drink or sweet, and whether any banned dye has been used.

items: One spot from a sample means the sample is a pure substance.
Two or more spots means it is a mixture, and the number of spots is the minimum number of substances present.
To identify what a mixture contains, run known reference substances on the same paper at the same time. Any spot in the mixture that lines up at the same height as a reference spot is that substance.
Some substances are colourless. They are made visible by spraying with a locating agent (such as ninhydrin for amino acids) or by viewing the paper under an ultraviolet lamp.

cards.title: Experiment 4: What Conditions Are Needed for Rusting?
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Aim: To find out whether iron needs air, water, or both, in order to rust.
Explanation: Materials: Three test tubes with bungs, three clean iron nails, boiled distilled water, cooking oil, anhydrous calcium chloride (a drying agent), tap water.
Explanation: Results after one week: Only the nail in tube A has rusted. The nails in tubes B and C are unchanged.
Painting — cheap and used on bridges, gates and car bodies; must be repaired if it chips.
Oiling or greasing — used on moving parts such as bicycle chains and machine tools.
Plastic coating — used on dish racks, garden furniture and fridge shelves.
Electroplating with chromium or tin — gives a shiny protective layer, used on taps and on food cans.
Galvanising — coating iron with zinc. Even if the coating is scratched, the zinc still protects the iron because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first.

cards.title: Experiment 6: Making Ethanol by Fermentation

Solvent — dissolves substances that will not dissolve in water, so it is used in perfumes, glues, inks, cosmetics and medicines.

Alcoholic drinks — the ethanol in beer, wine and spirits.
Antiseptic — used to sterilise skin and instruments because it kills bacteria.
