cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Health and disease are closely linked to population dynamics. Overcrowding, poor sanitation, malnutrition, and lack of healthcare contribute to the spread of diseases. In Africa, many diseases are preventable but remain major causes of death and disability.
Explanation: We will examine one disease from each of three groups: nutritional, water‑linked, and vector‑associated.

cards.title: Resettlement Overview
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Urbanisation is the process by which an increasing proportion of a country's population lives in towns and cities. It involves the growth of urban areas, both in number and in size, and the migration of people from rural to urban areas.
Explanation: Globally, more than half of the world's population now lives in urban areas. The process is fastest in developing countries, where cities are expanding rapidly.
Problems: poor planning, lack of resources, conflicts

cards.title: Quality of life
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Quality of life refers to the general well‑being of individuals and communities. It encompasses not only material wealth (income, housing) but also health, education, social connections, environment, and personal satisfaction.
Explanation: In this section, we compare the quality of life in rural and urban areas, using examples from Zimbabwe and other African countries.
Hierarchy: village → town → city → mega-city

cards.title: Problems in Settlement And Population Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Housing shortages: Informal settlements (slums) grow rapidly.
Unemployment: Not enough jobs for all migrants.
Traffic congestion: More vehicles, longer travel times.
Pollution: Air, water, and noise pollution affect health.
Inadequate services: Water, sanitation, electricity, and waste management are overwhelmed.
Crime and social problems: Inequality and anonymity can lead to crime.

cards.title: Solutions in Settlement And Population Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Urban planning: Zoning, green belts, and satellite towns.
Investment in infrastructure: Expand water, transport, and power networks.
Affordable housing schemes: Government-built flats and slum upgrading.
Job creation: Encourage industries and small businesses.
Decentralisation: Develop secondary cities and growth points to reduce pressure on mega-cities.
Environmental management: Pollution controls, recycling, and green spaces.

cards.title: Concentric Zone Model (Burgess, 1925)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Structure: City grows outward from a central business district (CBD) in a series of rings: 1. CBD (shops, offices, entertainment)
2. Zone of transition (industry, poor housing, slums)
3. Zone of working‑class homes (older terraced houses)
4. Zone of better housing (middle‑class suburbs)
5. Commuter zone (wealthy suburbs, rural‑urban fringe)
Assumptions: Flat land, free market, equal transport in all directions.

cards.title: Disadvantages in Settlement And Population Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: High cost of living (rent, transport, food).
Higher crime rates and social inequality.
Stress and lack of community spirit.
Work: Urban areas offer formal jobs, but many are in the informal sector. Rural work is mainly farming, often subsistence and weather‑dependent.
Health: Urban hospitals are better equipped, but overstretched. Rural clinics are scarce, and many rely on traditional healers. HIV/AIDS and malaria are significant challenges.
Education: Urban schools have better facilities and qualified teachers. Rural schools often lack resources, and children may drop out to help on farms.

o-level/form-4/geography/TransportAndTra.title: Transport And Trade Studies
snippets: Definition: Transport routes are the paths or lines along which people, goods, and services move. They include roads, railways, waterways, and air corridors. The development of these routes is essential for economic growth and regional integration.
In Africa, transport routes are often poorly developed compared to other continents. This is due to a mix of physical, economic, social, and political factors.
Definition: A transport network is a system of routes (lines) and junctions (nodes) that connect places. It is like a web that allows movement of people and goods.
Geographers use topological diagrams to simplify networks. A topological diagram ignores the real distance and shape and just shows connections. This helps to understand the structure.

cards.title: Transport And Trade Studies: Essential Terms
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: A transport network is a system of routes (lines) and junctions (nodes) that connect places. It is like a web that allows movement of people and goods.
Explanation: Geographers use topological diagrams to simplify networks. A topological diagram ignores the real distance and shape and just shows connections. This helps to understand the structure.
Transport route: path for movement (road, rail, water, air)
Colonial legacy: routes built for resource extraction
Route system: The actual physical layout of roads, railways, etc., on a map.

Topological diagram: A simplified map where only the connections (nodes and edges) matter. Think of a subway map (e.g., the London Tube map). The distances are not to scale; only the sequence of stops matters.
Nodes: Points where routes meet (e.g., towns, junctions, ports).
Edges: The routes (roads, rail lines) connecting the nodes.

cards.title: Network Overview
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°), which passes through Greenwich, London. The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so it moves 15° every hour (360° ÷ 24 = 15°).
Definition: This means that places east of Greenwich have a later local time, while places west have an earlier time. For example, Zimbabwe is at 30°E, so it is 2 hours ahead of GMT (30 ÷ 15 = 2).
Network: routes (edges) + junctions (nodes)
Accessibility: how easy to reach a node
Calculation of time difference: Divide the longitude difference by 15 to get the time difference in hours.
East = ahead: If you go east, you add hours.
West = behind: If you go west, you subtract hours.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Economic groupings (or trade blocs) are organisations of countries that agree to reduce trade barriers among themselves. They aim to promote economic integration, growth, and development.
Explanation: The spatial arrangement of groupings often follows geographic regions (neighbouring countries), but can also be political (e.g., COMECON).
International: colonial legacy, terms of trade

cards.title: Modern Transport in Transport And Trade Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Trade is the exchange of goods, services, or money between people, businesses, or countries. It allows people to get what they need or want that they do not produce themselves.

Explanation: Origins: Trade began in prehistoric times with bartering (exchanging goods directly, e.g., grain for meat). It grew with the development of civilisations (e.g., the Silk Road, Indian Ocean trade). Colonialism created global trade networks, often exploiting colonies for raw materials.

cards.title: Trade Overview
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Regional imbalances refer to the unequal distribution of wealth, resources, and economic activity between different areas (regions) within a country or between countries.
Definition: In trade terms, it means that some regions export valuable goods and become wealthy, while others export low‑value goods and remain poor.

cards.title: Node Accessibility in Transport And Trade Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Transport networks help us decide where to place new services like hospitals, clinics, schools, and settlements.
Definition: How easy it is to reach a node (town) from other nodes in the network.
Centrality: A central node (like a major city) has many connections and is highly accessible.
Isolated nodes: Remote villages with only one road connecting them have low accessibility.
Maximising accessibility: A new clinic should be placed at a node with high accessibility so that many people can reach it easily.
Serving isolated areas: Sometimes, a service is placed to serve a poorly connected area (rural hospital).
Network analysis: Using the topological diagram, planners can calculate the shortest path, travel times, and the number of people who can reach the new service within a certain time.

cards.title: Rail Transport in Transport And Trade Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Role: Heavy goods over long distances (coal, steel, grain). Also commuter transport in cities.
Changes: High‑speed rail (e.g., Shinkansen in Japan, TGV in France) competes with air travel for passenger traffic. Electrification reduces pollution.
GPS and SatNav: Helps drivers find the fastest routes, reducing travel time and fuel use.
Automation and AI: Autonomous ships, drones, and self‑driving trucks reduce labour costs and human error.
Electric and hybrid engines: Reduce reliance on fossil fuels, lowering carbon emissions.
Smart traffic management: Traffic lights and monitoring systems reduce congestion.

cards.title: International Trade in Transport And Trade Studies
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Exports: Goods or services sold to other countries (e.g., Zimbabwe exports minerals, tobacco, and gold).
Imports: Goods or services bought from other countries (e.g., Zimbabwe imports machinery, fuel, and electronics).
Balance of trade: The difference between the value of exports and imports. A surplus (exports > imports) is good; a deficit (imports > exports) can be a problem.
Zimbabwe: Main trading partners are South Africa, China, and the EU. Exports: gold, platinum, tobacco, nickel. Imports: fuels, machinery, chemicals.
Africa: Most African countries export primary products (raw materials) and import manufactured goods. This creates a colonial‑type trade pattern.
Intra‑African trade: Trade between African countries is low (about 15% of total trade) compared to Europe (60%). Reasons: poor infrastructure, colonial borders, and similar product bases.

items: Exports: Goods or services sold to other countries (e.g., Zimbabwe exports minerals, tobacco, and gold).

cards.title: International Level (between countries)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Colonial legacy: Former colonies are locked into exporting raw materials and importing expensive manufactured goods (unequal exchange).
Terms of trade: The ratio of export prices to import prices. If export prices fall (e.g., coffee) and import prices rise (e.g., machinery), the country gets poorer.
Trade barriers: Developed countries impose tariffs and subsidies that make it hard for developing countries to sell their goods (e.g., agricultural subsidies in the EU and USA).
Dependence on primary products: Most African countries rely on a few commodities (oil, minerals, coffee). Price fluctuations cause economic instability.
Debt: Countries with persistent trade deficits borrow money, leading to debt crises.
Dependency: Poor countries depend on rich countries for aid, loans, and markets.

blocks.title: Key points about International Level (between countries)
items: Colonial legacy: Former colonies are locked into exporting raw materials and importing expensive manufactured goods (unequal exchange).
Terms of trade: The ratio of export prices to import prices. If export prices fall (e.g., coffee) and import prices rise (e.g., machinery), the country gets poorer.
Trade barriers: Developed countries impose tariffs and subsidies that make it hard for developing countries to sell their goods (e.g., agricultural subsidies in the EU and USA).
Dependence on primary products: Most African countries rely on a few commodities (oil, minerals, coffee). Price fluctuations cause economic instability.
Debt: Countries with persistent trade deficits borrow money, leading to debt crises.
Dependency: Poor countries depend on rich countries for aid, loans, and markets.

cards.title: Transport And Trade Studies: What to Remember
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Transport routes in Africa are shaped by physical factors (relief, climate), economic needs (trade), social demands, and political history (colonialism).
• Transport networks are studied using topological diagrams. They help planners decide where to build schools and clinics based on accessibility.
• Longitude and time: Earth rotates 15° per hour. The IDL is at 180° – crossing west adds a day, crossing east subtracts a day.
• Modern transport uses technology (GPS, EVs, automation) to improve speed, cost, and safety, but causes environmental issues (pollution, congestion).
• Trade involves national (wholesale, retail) and international (exports, imports) exchange. Zimbabwe trades minerals and tobacco for machinery and fuel.
• Regional imbalances occur due to resource distribution, colonial history, and poor terms of trade, leading to debt and dependency.

cards.title: International Date Line (IDL)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The IDL is an imaginary line on the Earth's surface, roughly following the 180° meridian, where the date changes.
Crossing westwards (to Asia): You add a day (e.g., Monday becomes Tuesday).
Crossing eastwards (to the Americas): You subtract a day (e.g., Monday becomes Sunday).
Why it exists: To avoid confusion with time zones wrapping around the globe. It zigzags to avoid splitting countries or island groups.

o-level/form-4/geography/WeatherAndClima.title: Weather And Climate Studies
snippets: Definition: An air mass is a large body of air that has uniform temperature, humidity, and pressure characteristics. Air masses form over large areas of land or water called source regions. The characteristics of an air mass depend on the region where it forms.
Air masses are classified by their temperature (tropical, polar, arctic) and by their moisture content (maritime = wet, continental = dry).
Origins: Forms over the warm Indian Ocean and Atlantic Ocean, particularly near the tropics.

cards.title: Weather And Climate Studies: Essential Terms
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Rainfall occurs when moist air rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds. When the water droplets become too heavy, they fall as rain. There are four main types of rainfall:
Definition: Orographic rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. As the air rises, it cools, condenses, and forms clouds on the windward side of the mountain.
Definition: Convectional rainfall occurs when the sun heats the ground, causing the air above it to warm and rise. As the air rises, it cools, condenses, and forms clouds.
Air mass: large body of air with uniform characteristics
Tropical Maritime: warm, moist air from oceans
Tropical Continental: warm, dry air from land
Polar Maritime: cold, moist air from polar regions
Process: Moist air is forced up the mountain slope. It cools, condenses, and rain falls on the windward side. The leeward side (rain shadow) is dry.

cards.title: Depressions (Low Pressure Systems)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems that form over warm tropical oceans. They are characterised by strong winds, heavy rain, and storm surges.
Definition: A low-pressure system where air rises and moves inwards in an anticlockwise direction (in the Southern Hemisphere).
Weather sequence: Unstable weather, cloudiness, rainfall, and often strong winds.
Types: Mid-latitude depressions: Form between 30° and 60° latitude. Bring frontal rainfall.
Tropical cyclones: Form over warm oceans near the tropics. Bring destructive winds and heavy rainfall.
Formation: Warm ocean water (above 26.5°C), moist air, and the Coriolis effect. They form between 5° and 20° north and south of the equator.
Structure: Eye (calm centre), eye wall (strongest winds and heaviest rain), and spiral rain bands.

cards.title: Tangent to a Circle — Worked Example 1
points: Example: TA is a tangent at A to a circle, centre O. AB is a chord. If the angle between the tangent and the chord, BÂT, is x°, show that the angle BÔA is 2x°.
Step 1: Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, angle BÂO = (90 − x)°.
Step 2: Triangle AOB is isosceles, because OA and OB are both radii, so angle ABO is also (90 − x)°.
Step 3: The three angles of triangle AOB add up to 180°, so angle BÔA = 180° − 2(90 − x)°.

cards.title: Tangents from an External Point
points: Explanation: From any point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn to it. What's remarkable is that those two tangents always turn out to be exactly the same length — and the line joining the external point back to the centre always bisects both the angle between the tangents, and the angle between the two radii drawn to the points of contact.
Key rule: The two tangents drawn to a circle from the same external point are always equal in length.

cards.title: Tangents from an External Point — Worked Example 2
points: Example: O is the centre of a circle, and TA and TB are tangents from an external point T. If angle ATO = 39°, calculate angle TBX, where X is the point where the diagonals of quadrilateral TAOB cross.
Step 1: In triangle TAX, angle AXT = 90° (this follows from the symmetry of the figure — OT is the line of symmetry, so it crosses AB at right angles).
Step 2: The three angles of triangle TAX sum to 180°, so angle TAX = 180° − (90° + 39°) = 51°.
Step 3: By the same symmetry, angle TBX must equal angle TAX.
Answer: TBX = 51°

cards.title: Tangents from an External Point — Worked Example 3
points: Example: X, Y and Z are three points on a circle, centre O. The tangents to the circle at X and Y meet at T. If angle XTY = 58°, calculate angle XZY, where Z is on the major arc XY.
Step 1: In quadrilateral TXOY, both angle OXT and angle OYT are 90°, since a tangent is perpendicular to its radius.
Step 2: The angles of the quadrilateral sum to 360°, so angle XOY = 360° − 90° − 90° − 58° = 122°.
Step 3: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc, so angle XZY = half of 122°.
Answer: XZY = 61° (or 119° if Z is taken on the minor arc instead)

cards.title: Contact of Circles
points: Explanation: Two circles touch each other when they share a single common tangent at exactly the same point. That can happen in two different ways: the circles can sit side-by-side (touching externally), or one can nestle inside the other (touching internally). Either way, one fact never changes — the point where they touch always lies exactly on the straight line joining their two centres.

Definition: If two circles touch each other, the point of contact lies on the line of centres, and the distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii (external contact) or the difference of the radii (internal contact).

cards.title: Contact of Circles — Worked Example 4
points: Example: A, B and C are the centres of three circles that all touch each other externally. If AB = 13 cm, BC = 14 cm and CA = 11 cm, calculate the radius of each circle.
Step 1: Since every pair of circles touches externally, each distance between centres is the SUM of that pair's radii: a + b = 13, b + c = 14, c + a = 11 (using a, b, c for the radii at A, B, C).
Step 2: Subtracting the third equation from the second gives b − a = 3.
Step 3: Adding this to the first equation (a + b = 13) gives 2b = 16, so b = 8. Then a = 13 − 8 = 5, and c = 14 − 8 = 6.
Answer: The radii are 5 cm (A), 8 cm (B) and 6 cm (C).

cards.title: The Alternate Segment Theorem
points: Explanation: This is one of the most useful circle theorems for solving angle-chasing problems, because it connects an angle OUTSIDE the circle (between a tangent and a chord) to an angle INSIDE it (in the segment on the far side of that chord). Once you can spot a tangent and a chord meeting at the same point, this theorem hands you an equal angle somewhere else in the diagram for free.
Definition: If a straight line touches a circle, and a chord is drawn from the point of contact, then the angle between the tangent and the chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

cards.title: The Alternate Segment Theorem — Worked Example 5
points: Example: PQX is a tangent to a circle QRS at Q. If angle RSQ = 55° and angle RQX = 48°, calculate angle SQX.
Step 1: In triangle QRS, the three angles sum to 180°, so angle SQR = 180° − (55° + 48°) = 77°.
Answer: By the alternate segment theorem, SQX = SQR = 77°

cards.title: The Alternate Segment Theorem — Worked Example 6
points: Example: PT is a tangent to circle ABCT at T. BA = BT, and angle ATP = 82°. Calculate angle BCT.
Step 1: By the alternate segment theorem, angle ABT (in the alternate segment) equals angle ATP, so ABT = 82°.
Step 2: Triangle ABT is isosceles since BA = BT, so angle BAT = half of (180° − 82°) = 49°.
Step 3: ABTC is a cyclic quadrilateral, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, so angle BCT = 180° − angle BAT.

cards.title: Worked Example Library
points: Explanation: Every worked example from this chapter, gathered in one place. Use this page to revise the theorems by working through each solution again without the surrounding explanation, or to hunt for the closest match to a problem you're stuck on.

cards.title: Worked Example Library — Example 1 · Tangent ⊥ Radius
points: Example: TA is a tangent at A to a circle, centre O. AB is a chord. If the angle between the tangent and the chord, BÂT, is x°, show that the angle BÔA is 2x°.
Step 1: Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, angle BÂO = (90 − x)°.
Step 2: Triangle AOB is isosceles (OA = OB, both radii), so angle ABO is also (90 − x)°.
Step 3: The angles of triangle AOB sum to 180°, so BÔA = 180° − 2(90 − x)°.
Answer: BÔA = 2x°

cards.title: Worked Example Library — Example 2 · Tangents from a Point
points: Example: O is the centre of a circle, and TA and TB are tangents from an external point T. If angle ATO = 39°, calculate angle TBX (X is where the diagonals of TAOB cross).
Step 1: Angle AXT = 90°, from the symmetry of the figure about OT.
Step 2: In triangle TAX, angle TAX = 180° − (90° + 39°) = 51°.
Step 3: By symmetry, angle TBX = angle TAX.
Answer: TBX = 51°

o-level/form-4/mathematics/GeneralArithm.title: General Arithmetic
snippets: Explanation: Before you touch a calculator, a good mathematician always guesses the answer first. This guess is called a rough estimate. We are not trying to find the exact answer here — we only want a number that is close, so that if you press the wrong button on your calculator later, you will notice right away, because the real answer will look strange next to your guess.

More to know: The easiest way to make a rough estimate is to round every number in the problem to just 1 significant figure — that means keeping only the very first digit and turning the rest into zeros. Then you do the simple sum in your head.

cards.title: Rough Estimates and Checking Your Work
points: Explanation: Before you touch a calculator, a good mathematician always guesses the answer first. This guess is called a rough estimate. We are not trying to find the exact answer here — we only want a number that is close, so that if you press the wrong button on your calculator later, you will notice right away, because the real answer will look strange next to your guess.

More to know: The easiest way to make a rough estimate is to round every number in the problem to just 1 significant figure — that means keeping only the very first digit and turning the rest into zeros. Then you do the simple sum in your head.

cards.title: Rough Estimates and Checking Your Work — Worked Example
points: Example: Find a rough estimate for 39.8 × 5.2.
Step 1: Round 39.8 to 1 significant figure → 40.
Step 2: Round 5.2 to 1 significant figure → 5.
Step 3: Multiply the rounded numbers: 40 × 5 = 200.
Answer: ≈ 200

cards.title: Rough Estimates and Checking Your Work — Worked Example
points: Example: A calculator shows 3120 ÷ 58 = 53.79. Use estimation to check if this looks reasonable.
Step 1: Round 3120 to 1 significant figure → 3000.
Step 2: Round 58 to 1 significant figure → 60.
Step 3: Divide the rounded numbers: 3000 ÷ 60 = 50.
Step 4: 50 is close to 53.79, so the calculator answer is reasonable.
Answer: Reasonable ✓ (estimate ≈ 50)

cards.title: Rounding Off Numbers
points: Explanation: Rounding means changing a number to a simpler, nearby number that is easier to work with — to the nearest ten, the nearest hundred, the nearest whole number, or to a set number of decimal places. Think of it like a ball sitting on a hill between two valleys. If the ball is more than halfway down one side, it rolls all the way to that side. If it hasn't even reached halfway, it rolls back to where it started.
More to know: That is exactly the rule for rounding: look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to. If it is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 — round up. If it is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 — leave it the same.

cards.title: Rounding Off Numbers — Worked Example
points: Example: Round 3456 to the nearest hundred.
Step 1: Find the hundreds digit: the 4 in 3456.
Step 2: Look at the next digit (the tens digit): 5.
Step 3: 5 is "5 or more", so we round the 4 up to a 5.
Step 4: Change the rest of the digits to zero.
Answer: 3500

cards.title: Rounding Off Numbers — Worked Example
points: Example: Round 4.567 to 2 decimal places.
Step 1: Count 2 digits after the decimal point: 4.56 | 7.
Step 2: Look at the next digit: 7.
Step 3: 7 is 5 or more, so the 6 rounds up to a 7.
Step 4: Drop everything after that.
Answer: 4.57

cards.title: Significant Figures in General Arithmetic
points: Explanation: Significant figures are the digits in a number that carry real, meaningful information about how carefully it was measured. Counting them is a bit like counting the important people standing in a photograph — you skip the empty space at the edges (leading zeros), but you count everyone in the middle, even the quiet one wearing a plain zero shirt.

cards.title: Significant Figures — Worked Example
points: Example: Round 0.004821 to 2 significant figures.
Step 1: The leading zeros do not count, so the first significant figure is 4.
Step 2: The second significant figure is 8.
Step 3: Look at the next digit: 2. This is less than 5, so 8 stays the same.
Answer: 0.0048

cards.title: Significant Figures — Worked Example
points: Example: Round 3050 to 2 significant figures.
Step 1: The first two significant figures are 3 and 0.
Step 2: Look at the next digit: 5.
Step 3: 5 rounds the second figure up: 0 becomes 1.
Step 4: Replace the remaining digits with zeros to keep the size of the number correct.
Answer: 3100

cards.title: Limits of Accuracy
points: Explanation: No measurement is ever perfectly exact — not even the best ruler, scale or tape measure. They can only measure to a certain 'nearest unit'. If someone tells you a stick is 23.8 cm long, they really mean: 'the true length is very close to 23.8 cm — it could be a tiny bit more, or a tiny bit less.'

More to know: We call this the limits of accuracy: an Upper Bound (the biggest the true value could possibly be) and a Lower Bound (the smallest it could possibly be). The true value always sits somewhere between the two.

cards.title: Limits of Accuracy — Worked Example
points: Example: A measurement is given as 23.8 cm, to the nearest 0.1 cm. Find the upper and lower bounds.
Step 1: The smallest unit used is 0.1 cm.
Step 2: Half of 0.1 cm is 0.05 cm.
Step 3: Upper bound = 23.8 + 0.05 = 23.85 cm.
Step 4: Lower bound = 23.8 − 0.05 = 23.75 cm.
Answer: Lower bound = 23.75 cm, Upper bound = 23.85 cm

cards.title: Limits of Accuracy — Worked Example
points: Example: A bag of maize meal is labelled 50 kg, weighed to the nearest kg. Find the limits of accuracy.
Step 1: The smallest unit is 1 kg.
Step 2: Half of 1 kg is 0.5 kg.
Step 3: Upper bound = 50 + 0.5 = 50.5 kg.
Step 4: Lower bound = 50 − 0.5 = 49.5 kg.
Answer: 49.5 kg ≤ true mass < 50.5 kg

o-level/form-4/mathematics/GeometricalCo.title: Geometrical Constructions
snippets: Explanation: In this chapter we draw shapes using only two tools: a ruler (for straight lines) and a pair of compasses (for arcs and circles) — no protractor allowed! Every construction below is built from real, exact arcs, so you can trust every crossing point completely. Press play on each one and watch it happen, step by step, with the working written out as it goes.

cards.title: Basic Constructions: Bisectors and Right Angles
points: Explanation: In this chapter we draw shapes using only two tools: a ruler (for straight lines) and a pair of compasses (for arcs and circles) — no protractor allowed! Every construction below is built from real, exact arcs, so you can trust every crossing point completely. Press play on each one and watch it happen, step by step, with the working written out as it goes.

cards.title: Basic Constructions: Bisectors and Right Angles — Worked Example
points: Example: Why must you keep the compass width exactly the same when drawing the two crossing arcs in a bisector construction?
Step 1: If the width changed between arcs, the new crossing point would not be equally distant from both original points (or both arms).
Step 2: Keeping the width the same is what guarantees the construction is accurate.
Answer: Because the equal width is what makes the resulting line truly perpendicular / a true bisector.

cards.title: Basic Constructions: Triangles, Copying Angles, and Special Angles
points: Explanation: Some angles come up so often in geometry that it helps to know how to build them directly with compasses alone — no protractor, no guessing. The trick for 45° and 30° is simple: build a bigger angle you already know how to make (90° or 60°), then bisect it.

cards.title: Basic Constructions: Triangles, Copying Angles, and Special Angles — Worked Example
points: Example: You need a 15° angle for a technical drawing, but your protractor is broken. How could you construct one using only compasses?
Step 1: Construct a 60° angle (using the equilateral triangle method).
Step 2: Bisect it to get 30°.
Step 3: Bisect the 30° angle again — bisecting cuts any angle exactly in half.
Answer: Bisect 60° down to 30°, then bisect 30° down to 15°.

cards.title: Constructing Parallel Lines, and a Perpendicular from an External Point
points: Explanation: Sometimes the point you need a perpendicular from is not sitting on the line at all — it's off to one side. And sometimes you need a brand new line that never meets a given one, no matter how far it is extended: a parallel line. Both of these are just clever uses of the constructions you already know.

cards.title: Constructing Parallel Lines, and a Perpendicular from an External Point — Worked Example
points: Example: Why does making the two angles at Q and P equal guarantee that the new line through P is parallel to AB?
Step 1: When a transversal crosses two lines and the corresponding angles are equal, the two lines can never meet, however far they are extended.
Step 2: This is the corresponding-angles rule for parallel lines.
Answer: Equal corresponding angles is the defining test for two lines being parallel.

cards.title: What Is a Locus? The Five Common Loci
points: Explanation: A locus is simply the path traced out by every possible position of a point that follows one particular rule. The word is Latin for "place" — mathematicians use it for the set of ALL the places a point is allowed to be. Some rules give a straight line. Some give a circle. Some give something in between. Below are the five loci you must know for this course — press play on each one to see the shape being built, and then watch a point slide along it to prove the rule really does hold everywhere.
Definition: "A locus is the set of all possible positions occupied by a point which varies its position according to some given rule."

cards.title: What Is a Locus? The Five Common Loci — Worked Example
points: Example: A security light is fixed to a wall and needs to shine on any point exactly 5 m away from it. What shape is the locus of points it can reach?
Step 1: The rule is "a fixed distance from one fixed point".
Step 2: This is our first common locus.
Answer: A circle of radius 5 m, centred on the light.

cards.title: Construction of Loci: Combining Two Rules
points: Explanation: Many real problems give you TWO rules at once, and ask for the position (or positions) that satisfy both together. The method is always the same: construct each locus separately, on the same diagram, and then simply look for where they cross. Every crossing point is a valid answer.

cards.title: Construction of Loci: Combining Two Rules — Worked Example
points: Example: A buried cable runs in a straight line across a field. A farmer wants to plant a tree that is both at least 3 m from the cable, AND the same distance from two gate posts at either end of the field. Describe how to find every possible spot.
Step 1: Draw the locus for "3 m from the cable" — this is a pair of parallel lines, one on each side.
Step 2: Draw the locus for "equidistant from the two gate posts" — this is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
Step 3: Any point where these two loci cross satisfies both conditions at once.
Answer: The tree can go at any crossing point between the parallel-line locus and the perpendicular bisector.

cards.title: The Circumcircle of a Triangle
points: Explanation: Here is a beautiful result that comes straight from what you've already learned: if you construct the perpendicular bisector of every side of a triangle, all three bisectors meet at exactly the same single point. That point — called the circumcentre — is equally distant from all three corners of the triangle, so a circle drawn from there passes through all three corners perfectly.
Definition: The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides of any triangle always meet at one point — the circumcentre — which is the centre of the circle passing through all three vertices.

cards.title: The Circumcircle of a Triangle — Worked Example
points: Example: Would the circumcentre of a very "flat", obtuse-angled triangle still be found the same way?
Step 1: Yes — the method (construct two perpendicular bisectors, find where they meet) works for every triangle.
Step 2: For an obtuse triangle, the circumcentre actually ends up OUTSIDE the triangle, rather than inside it.
Answer: Same method every time — but for an obtuse triangle, the circumcentre lies outside the triangle.

points: Example: A'(0;0), B'(-5;6), C'(-2;-9) are the images of A(0;0), B(5;2), C(2;-3) under a transformation represented by a matrix of the form [[a,0],[0,b]]. (a) Find the transformation matrix. (b) Find the matrix which will transform △A'B'C' back to △ABC.

points: Example: Triangle OAB has vertices O(0;0), A(2;1), B(0;2). It is enlarged by factor 2 with origin as centre, then translated by vector (-3;-5). Find the coordinates of the image.

points: Example: The rhombus whose vertices are at (0;0), (1;2), (3;3) and (2;1) is first reflected in the x-axis and then sheared by the operator [[1,2],[0,1]]. Find the vertices of the resulting figure.

cards.title: Composition of Matrix Transformations — Worked Example
points: Example: (a,b) is the image of a point (a;b) after a transformation given by [[4,0],[0,3]] (a;b) + (-7;-2). (a) Describe the transformation in words. (b) A' is the image of A(-1;2). Find the coordinates of A'. (c) Find the coordinates of a point B which has an image at B'(5;-5).
Answer: (a) stretch by 4 in x, 3 in y, then translate (-7,-2); (b) A'(-11;4); (c) B(3;-1)

points: Explanation: A sketch graph is a simple freehand drawing which shows the main features of a line or curve. These features are typically the intercepts on the axes and the general shape.

cards.title: Linear, Quadratic and Inverse Functions — Worked Example

cards.title: Statistics (5) Grouped Data
points: Explanation: When statistical data contain a large number of values, it is impractical to draw a bar chart and often difficult to calculate averages. The data can be reduced to a frequency distribution.

cards.title: Statistics (5) Grouped Data — Worked Example
points: Example: The number of schools in twelve towns is as follows: 1 town has 4 schools, 4 towns have 5 schools, 2 towns have 6 schools, 3 towns have 7 schools, and 2 towns have 8 schools. (a) State the mode and median. (b) Calculate the mean.
Answer: Mode = 5, Median = 6, Mean = 5

o-level/form-4/mathematics/GraphsGradien.title: Graphs Gradient
snippets: Gradient of AB = increase in y ⁄ increase in x = tan θ = θ (with the positive x-direction) ≈ °
rearranges to y = x + so the gradient is.
Once an equation is in the form y = mx + c, the coefficient of x is always the gradient — no measuring required.

cards.title: Gradient of a Straight Line
points: Explanation: In Fig. 5.1, HG is a horizontal line and HK makes an angle θ with HG. Triangles ABC, PQR, UVW along the slope are all similar, so the ratio BC ⁄ AB is the same wherever it is measured along the line — this constant ratio is called the gradient. It also equals tan θ, since BC ⁄ AB is exactly the tangent ratio in each right-angled triangle. Drag the slider below to see the gradient triangle stretch and flip as the line's steepness and direction change.
Key rule: Gradient of a line = (increase in y) ⁄ (increase in x), measured between any two points on it.
Key rule: Gradient = tan θ, where θ is the angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis.
Key rule: Gradient of the line through (x₁; y₁) and (x₂; y₂) = (y₂ − y₁) ⁄ (x₂ − x₁).

cards.title: Gradient of a Straight Line — Worked Example 1
points: Example: Find the gradients of the lines joining (a) A(−1; 2) and B(3; −2), (b) C(0; −1) and D(4; 1).
Step 1: Gradient = (difference in y-coordinates) ÷ (difference in x-coordinates).
Step 3: (b) Gradient of CD = (1 − (−1)) ÷ (4 − 0) = 2 ÷ 4 = ½.
Answer: (a) −1 (b) ½

cards.title: Drawing a Graph from an Equation
points: Explanation: To draw the line represented by an equation like 4x + 2y = 5, first build a table of values (choose a few x-values and calculate the matching y), plot the points, and draw the straight line through them. The gradient can then be read off by taking measurements from the finished graph — or, as the next section shows, straight from the equation itself. Try each preset equation below and watch the table and line update together.

cards.title: Drawing a Graph from an Equation — Worked Example 2
points: Example: Draw a graph of the line represented by 4x + 2y = 5, and find its gradient by taking measurements.
Step 1: Make a table of values: when x = 0, y = 2½; when x = 1, y = ½; when x = 2, y = −1½.
Step 2: Plot these points and draw the straight line through them.
Step 3: Choose two convenient points on the drawn line, e.g. (0, 2½) and (2, −1½).
Step 4: Gradient = increase in y ÷ increase in x = −4 ÷ 2 = −2.
Answer: Gradient = −2

cards.title: Sketching Graphs of Straight Lines
points: Explanation: Once an equation is rearranged into the form y = mx + c, the coefficient of x, m, gives the gradient directly, and c is the y-intercept — no measuring needed. Two quick sketching methods follow from this: use the gradient and one point (fastest when the y-intercept is easy to find), or find both axis intercepts and join them (fastest for equations like ax + by = c). A line parallel to the x-axis (y = constant) has zero gradient; a line parallel to the y-axis (x = constant) has an undefined gradient, since the increase in x is always zero. Try each case below.
Key rule: If y = mx + c, the gradient of the line is m and it crosses the y-axis at (0, c).
Key rule: A line parallel to the x-axis has the form y = c and has zero gradient.
Key rule: A line parallel to the y-axis has the form x = a and has an undefined (infinite) gradient.

cards.title: Sketching Graphs of Straight Lines — Worked Example 3
points: Example: Make a rough sketch of the line whose equation is 2x + 4y = 9.
Step 1: Rearrange to make y the subject: 4y = −2x + 9, so y = −½x + 2¼.
Step 2: Find a point on the line — the simplest is where x = 0: when x = 0, y = 2¼.
Step 3: Plot (0, 2¼), then use the gradient −½ to step to a second point and draw the line.
Answer: y = −½x + 2¼, sketch through (0, 2¼) with gradient −½

cards.title: Sketching Graphs of Straight Lines — Worked Example 4
points: Example: Sketch the graph of the line whose equation is 4x − 3y = 12.
Step 1: When x = 0: −3y = 12, so y = −4. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, −4).
Step 2: When y = 0: 4x = 12, so x = 3. The line crosses the x-axis at (3, 0).
Step 3: Join the two intercepts with a ruler to complete the sketch.
Answer: Crosses the axes at (0, −4) and (3, 0)

cards.title: Finding the Equation of a Straight Line
points: Explanation: There are two common starting points for finding a line's equation: (a) a gradient and one point on the line, or (b) two points on the line. Both methods rest on the same idea — pick a general point (x, y) on the line, write down its gradient to a known point, and set that equal to the known gradient (found directly, or by using the two given points).
Key rule: Given gradient m through point (a; b): (y − b) ⁄ (x − a) = m.
Key rule: Given two points (a; b) and (c; d): (y − b) ⁄ (x − a) = (d − b) ⁄ (c − a).

cards.title: Finding the Equation of a Straight Line — Worked Example 5
points: Example: A straight line of gradient 5 passes through the point B(3; −8). Find the equation of the line.
Step 1: Let A(x, y) be any general point on the line.
Step 2: Gradient of AB = (y − (−8)) ÷ (x − 3) = (y + 8) ⁄ (x − 3).
Step 3: Since the gradient of AB is 5, (y + 8) ⁄ (x − 3) = 5.
Answer: y = 5x − 23

cards.title: Finding the Equation of a Straight Line — Worked Example 6
points: Example: Find the equation of the straight line which passes through the points Q(−1; 7) and R(3; −2).
Step 2: Let P(x, y) be any general point on the line. Gradient of PR = (y − (−2)) ⁄ (x − 3) = (y + 2) ⁄ (x − 3).
Step 3: Since PQR is a straight line, gradient of PR = gradient of QR: (y + 2) ⁄ (x − 3) = −2¼.
Step 4: y + 2 = −2¼(x − 3) = −2¼x + 6¾, so y = −2¼x + 4¾.
Answer: y = −2¼x + 4¾

cards.title: Gradient of a Curve
points: Explanation: The gradient of a straight line is the same at every point on it, but the gradient of a curve changes from point to point. The gradient at a particular point on a curve is defined as the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point — a ruler placed against the curve so the angles it makes with the curve on either side look equal. Slide the point along either curve below to watch the tangent (and its gradient) update continuously.
Definition: The gradient of a curve at a point equals the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curve at that point.

cards.title: Gradient of a Curve — Worked Example 7
points: Example: Fig. 5.15 shows the curve y = 2 + x − x² for x from −2 to 3. Using the tangents drawn at P and Q, find the gradient of the curve at (a) P, (b) Q.
Step 1: The gradient of a curve at a point is defined as the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point.
Step 2: At P, using the right-angled triangle TOP formed by the tangent: gradient = OP ÷ TO = 2 ÷ 2 = 1.
Step 3: At Q, using triangle QMR formed the same way: gradient = −MR ÷ QM = −3 ÷ 1 = −3.
Step 4: Use the interactive tangent demo above (choose "y = 2 + x − x²") to see this tangent-drawing idea in action at any point on the curve.
Answer: (a) 1 (b) −3

o-level/form-4/mathematics/Inequalities.title: Inequalities
snippets: Think of it like planning a shopping trip. You have a fixed budget, and you need to buy different items. Each item costs a certain amount, and you have to stay within your budget. But you also want to get the most items, or the most value.

Each restriction — like the budget, or the number of items you can carry — can be written as an inequality. When you put all the inequalities together, they create a region on a graph. The points inside that region are all the possible solutions.
The best solution — like the one that gives you the most items or the lowest cost — is found by looking at the edges of that region. This is what we call linear programming.
Now let's look at a real problem. A student has $2.50 to spend on ballpens and pencils.

cards.title: Linear Programming in Inequalities
points: Definition: Linear programming is a method for finding the best outcome (such as maximum profit or lowest cost) in a mathematical model whose requirements are represented by linear relationships.

o-level/form-4/mathematics/Probabilities.title: Probabilities
snippets: These are examples of combined probabilities. Before we start combining events, let's quickly remind ourselves how probability works.
Probability can be found by comparing the number of outcomes we want with the number of possible outcomes. For example, a fair die has 6 possible outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
There is only one way to roll a 5. So the probability of rolling a 5 is 1/6. This is called theoretical probability because we calculate it from the possible outcomes.

We can also use what has happened in the past. Imagine that it rained in Gwanda during 9 out of 12 Septembers. Based on those past results, we could estimate the probability of rain next September as 9/12 = ¾. This is called experimental probability because it is based on observations or past data.

cards.title: Probability (2) – Combined Probabilities
points: Definition: For an event R: P(R) = n(R) / n(ℰ), where n(R) is the number of favourable outcomes and n(ℰ) is the number of all possible outcomes.

cards.title: Worked Examples in Probabilities

points: Explanation: These are examples of combined probabilities. Before we start combining events, let's quickly remind ourselves how probability works.
What is the probability of getting a 6 and then a 4 when rolling a die twice?
What is the probability of getting a head or a tail when tossing a coin?
What is the probability that two things happen together?

cards.title: The General Rule
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time. For example, choosing a vowel (A,E,I,O,U) and choosing one of X,Y,Z from the alphabet – no letter is both.
Explanation: Two events are independent if the outcome of one does not affect the other. For example, throwing a die and tossing a coin: getting a six does not affect getting a head.
Explanation: When there are many outcomes, tables and tree diagrams help us count them systematically.

snippets: Explanation: The cosine rule is used to solve a triangle when two sides and the angle between them (the included angle) are known, or when all three sides are known. Watch each line get written in, one step at a time — with the triangle itself drawn above it, ruler and protractor in hand.

cards.title: The Cosine Rule
points: Explanation: The cosine rule is used to solve a triangle when two sides and the angle between them (the included angle) are known, or when all three sides are known. Watch each line get written in, one step at a time — with the triangle itself drawn above it, ruler and protractor in hand.

cards.title: The Cosine Rule — Worked Example
points: Example: Find AB in the triangle where BC = 3 cm, CA = 2 cm and angle C = 80°.
Answer: AB ≈ 3,3 cm

cards.title: The Cosine Rule — Worked Example
points: Example: Find y in the triangle where the two sides from the apex are 5 cm and 3 cm, with a 102° angle between them.
Answer: y ≈ 6,34 cm

cards.title: Solving Triangles Using the Sine and Cosine Rules
points: Explanation: Once the cosine rule has found one missing side, the sine rule is often the quickest way to find the remaining angles. Always find the smaller of the two unknown angles first, since that angle is guaranteed to be acute — this avoids the ambiguous case where sin⁻¹ could mean two different angles.

cards.title: Solving Triangles Using the Sine and Cosine Rules — Worked Example
points: Example: In triangle ABC, a = 6,7 cm, c = 2,3 cm and B = 46,6°. Find b, A and C.

cards.title: Using the Cosine Rule to Calculate Angles
points: Explanation: When all three sides of a triangle are given, the cosine rule can be rearranged to make each cosine the subject in turn. It is advisable to find every angle this way, then check the three results add to 180°.

cards.title: Using the Cosine Rule to Calculate Angles — Worked Example
points: Example: Calculate the angles of a triangle with sides 4 m, 5 m and 7 m (AC = 5, CB = 4, AB = 7).

cards.title: Using the Cosine Rule to Calculate Angles — Worked Example
points: Example: Calculate the angles of triangles with sides (a) 400 m, 500 m, 700 m; (b) 2,8 cm, 4,2 cm, 5,6 cm.
Answer: (a) same angles as Example 5: 34,0°, 44,4°, 101,5° (b) solve 2: 3: 4

cards.title: Diagonals of Parallelograms and Cyclic Quadrilaterals
points: Explanation: A diagonal splits a parallelogram or a cyclic quadrilateral into two triangles that share a side. Because adjacent angles in a parallelogram are supplementary (they add to 180°), the cosine of one angle is always the negative of the other.

cards.title: Diagonals of Parallelograms and Cyclic Quadrilaterals — Worked Example
points: Example: The sides of a parallelogram are 7 cm and 10 cm and one diagonal, BD, is 15 cm. Find the length of the other diagonal, AC.
Answer: AC ≈ 8,54 cm

cards.title: Bearings and Distances
points: Explanation: A bearing problem becomes an ordinary triangle problem the moment the compass bearings are converted into an included angle between two known distances.

cards.title: Bearings and Distances — Worked Example
points: Example: Towns A, B and C are such that AB = 60 km and AC = 100 km. The bearing of B from A is 060° and the bearing of C from A is 290°. Calculate (a) the distance BC, (b) the bearing of B from C.
Answer: (a) BC ≈ 146 km (b) bearing of B from C ≈ 091,7°

P and Q are mirror images across Oy, so ON is shared by both — that's the whole proof.
A three-figure bearing always has three digits and is measured clockwise from north. The compass form measures away from N or S, toward E or W.

cards.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Obtuse Angles
points: Explanation: So far, sin, cos and tan have only been defined inside a right-angled triangle — which only works for acute angles. To handle obtuse angles too, picture a radius OP of length r, sweeping anticlockwise from the positive x-axis through angle θ. Drop P's projections onto both axes — OM onto Ox, ON onto Oy — and redefine the ratios in terms of those projections. Try sweeping θ past 90° below and watch what happens to each ratio.
Key rule: sin θ = projection of OP on Oy ⁄ OP, cos θ = projection of OP on Ox ⁄ OP, tan θ = projection on Oy ⁄ projection on Ox.

cards.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Obtuse Angles — Worked Example 1
points: Example: Find θ, where 0° ≤ θ ≤ 180°, given: (a) cos θ = 0.3420 (b) sin θ = 0.8988 (c) cos θ = −0.6157 (d) tan θ = −1.7321.
Step 1: (a) cos θ is positive, so θ is acute: θ = 70°.
Step 2: (b) sin θ = 0.8988 gives an acute angle of 64° — but sin(180° − 64°) = sin 64° too, so θ = 64° or 116°.
Step 3: (c) cos θ is negative, so θ is obtuse. The acute angle with cosine 0.6157 is 52°, so θ = 180° − 52°.
Step 4: (d) tan θ is negative, so θ is obtuse. The acute angle with tangent 1.7321 is 60°, so θ = 180° − 60°.

cards.title: The Supplementary Angle Identities
points: Explanation: Two points on the same circle, symmetric about the vertical axis, sit at angles θ and (180° − θ). Because they're mirror images, their projections onto Oy are identical — but their projections onto Ox are opposite in sign. That single observation proves all three identities below.
Key rule: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ
Key rule: cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ
Key rule: tan(180° − θ) = −tan θ

cards.title: Proving the Sine Rule
points: Explanation: Drop a perpendicular from one vertex of a triangle to the opposite side, and two right-angled triangles appear, sharing that perpendicular as a common height. Writing sin of each base angle in terms of that shared height links two sides and their opposite angles together — and the same trick works for every pair of sides, giving one continuous chain of equal ratios.
Key rule: a ⁄ sin A = b ⁄ sin B = c ⁄ sin C, where a, b, c are the sides opposite angles A, B, C.

cards.title: Solving Triangles Completely
points: Explanation: "Solve the triangle completely" means finding every missing side and angle. The sine rule handles two situations: two angles and any side (subtract from 180° for the third angle, then use the rule directly), or two sides and the angle opposite one of them — which is trickier, since it can sometimes produce two different valid triangles from the same data. Watch for that ambiguous case in Examples 3 and 4.

Definition: The sine rule solves a triangle when given either (i) two angles and any side, or (ii) two sides and the angle opposite one of them — though case (ii) can have two solutions, one solution, or none.

cards.title: Solving Triangles Completely — Worked Example 2
points: Example: In triangle ABC, B = 39°, C = 82°, a = 6.73 cm. Solve the triangle completely.
Step 2: By the sine rule, c ⁄ sin C = a ⁄ sin A.
Step 4: Similarly, b = (6.73 × sin 39°) ⁄ sin 59° ≈ 4.94 cm.
Answer: A = 59°, b ≈ 4.94 cm, c ≈ 7.78 cm

cards.title: Solving Triangles Completely — Worked Example 3
points: Example: In triangle ABC, a = 12.5 cm, c = 17.7 cm, C = 116°. Find the remaining angles.
Step 1: sin A ⁄ a = sin C ⁄ c, so sin A = (12.5 × sin 116°) ⁄ 17.7 = 0.6347.
Step 2: This gives A = 39.4° or A = 140.6° — but a triangle can only have one obtuse angle, and C is already obtuse, so A must be acute.

cards.title: Solving Triangles Completely — Worked Example 4
points: Example: In triangle ABC, a = 7.1 cm, b = 9.5 cm, B = 63°18′. Solve the triangle completely.
Step 1: sin A ⁄ a = sin B ⁄ b, so sin A = (7.1 × sin 63.3°) ⁄ 9.5 = 0.6683.
Step 2: This gives A = 41.89° or A = 138.11° — but since a < b, angle A must be smaller than angle B (63.3°), ruling out the obtuse option.
Step 4: c ⁄ sin C = b ⁄ sin B, so c = (9.5 × sin 74.81°) ⁄ sin 63.3° ≈ 10.26 cm.

cards.title: Bearings and Distances
points: Explanation: A three-figure bearing measures a direction clockwise from north, always written with three digits — 072°, not 72°. The same direction can be written as a compass bearing instead, like N72°E, measuring the angle away from north or south, toward east or west. Bearings problems almost always boil down to an ordinary triangle — the compass directions just tell you which angles to mark.
Definition: A bearing is always measured clockwise from north and written as three digits, e.g. 053°, 090°, 246°.

cards.title: Bearings and Distances — Worked Example 5
points: Example: A ship sails 8 km due east from A to B. From A, a lighthouse L bears 062°; from B, L bears 296°. Find the distance BL.
Step 1: At A, the angle between due east (AB) and AL is 90° − 62° = 28°.
Step 2: At B, the angle between due west (BA) and BL is 296° − 270° = 26°.
Step 3: So angle ALB = 180° − 28° − 26° = 126°.
Step 4: By the sine rule, BL ⁄ sin 28° = AB ⁄ sin 126°, so BL = (8 × sin 28°) ⁄ sin 126° ≈ 4.64 km.
Answer: BL ≈ 4.64 km

cards.title: Bearings and Distances — Worked Example 6
points: Example: Two straight roads meet at junction O at 55°. Peg P is 120 m from O along one road. On the other road, point Q is placed so that angle OQP = 82°. Find PQ.
Step 2: By the sine rule, PQ ⁄ sin O = OP ⁄ sin Q.
Answer: PQ ≈ 99.3 m

points: Explanation: Every worked example from this chapter, gathered in one place. Use this page to revise the sine rule's two use-cases — and the bearings problems that lean on it — without the surrounding explanation, or to find the closest match to a problem you're stuck on.

o-level/form-4/mathematics/Variation.title: Variation
snippets: Because D is directly proportional to T, if we double T, D also doubles. The constant of proportionality is 16, so D = 16T.
The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 16.
The graph is a hyperbola that never touches the axes.
Joint variation combines multiple direct proportionalities into one equation.

cards.title: Direct Variation in Variation
points: Explanation: Direct variation describes a relationship where one quantity is a constant multiple of another. If y is directly proportional to x, then y = kx for some constant k. This means that if x doubles, y also doubles; if x is halved, y is halved. The graph of y against x is a straight line through the origin. In this section, we explore the concept, the constant of proportionality, and how to solve problems involving direct variation.
Key rule: If y ∝ x then y = kx for some constant k (the constant of variation).
Key rule: The graph of y = kx is a straight line through the origin with gradient k.
Key rule: To find k, substitute known values of x and y into the equation.

cards.title: Direct Variation — Worked Example 1
points: Example: If D ∝ T and D = 80 when T = 5, find (a) the relationship between D and T, (b) the value of T when D = 56.
Step 1: Since D ∝ T, D = kT for some constant k.
Step 2: When D = 80, T = 5: 80 = k × 5, so k = 16.
Step 3: (a) The relationship is D = 16T.
Answer: (a) D = 16T (b) T = 3½

cards.title: Direct Variation — Worked Example 2
points: Example: Table 9.1 shows the extension E cm in an elastic string when pulled by a force of T newtons. (a) Show that E is directly proportional to T. (b) Find the value of E when T = 8.
Step 1: If E ∝ T, then E/T should have a constant value.
Step 4: Since E/T = 1.5 in both cases, E is directly proportional to T.
Answer: (a) Shown (b) E = 12

cards.title: Inverse Variation in Variation
points: Explanation: Inverse variation occurs when one quantity increases while the other decreases at a proportional rate. If y is inversely proportional to x, then y = k/x for some constant k. This means the product xy is always constant. The graph of y against x is a hyperbola that approaches both axes but never touches them. In this section, we explain the concept, how to find the constant, and how to solve problems involving inverse variation.
Key rule: If y ∝ 1/x then y = k/x for some constant k, and xy = k.
Key rule: The graph of y = k/x is a hyperbola approaching both axes.
Key rule: To find k, substitute known values of x and y.

cards.title: Inverse Variation — Worked Example 5
points: Example: If V varies inversely with n and V = 220 when n = 6, find V when n = 8.
Step 1: V = k/n for some constant k.
Answer: V = 165

cards.title: Inverse Variation — Worked Example 6
points: Example: The number of spherical glass beads which can be made from a given volume of glass varies inversely with the cube of the diameter. When d = 2 mm, N = 2700. How many beads of diameter 3 mm can be made?
Step 1: N ∝ 1/d³, so N = k/d³.
Step 3: N = 21600/d³.
Answer: 800 beads

cards.title: Joint Variation in Variation
points: Explanation: Joint variation involves more than two variables, where one quantity varies directly as the product of two or more other quantities. For example, the mass of a wire varies jointly with its length and the square of its diameter: M ∝ L d². This means M = k L d² for some constant k. If you double the length, the mass doubles; if you double the diameter, the mass quadruples (because d is squared). In this section, we explain how to set up joint variation equations, find the constant, and solve multi-step problems.
Key rule: If z ∝ xy then z = kxy for some constant k.
Key rule: To find k, substitute known values of all variables.
Key rule: You can combine joint variation with other types (e.g., y ∝ x/z²) by using constants and substitution.

cards.title: Joint Variation — Worked Example 7
points: Example: The mass of a wire varies jointly with its length and the square of its diameter. 500 m of wire of diameter 3 mm has a mass of 31.5 kg. What is the mass of 1 km of wire of diameter 2 mm?
Step 1: M ∝ Ld², so M = kLd².
Step 3: M = 0.007Ld².
Answer: 28 kg

cards.title: Joint Variation — Worked Example 8
points: Example: If X ∝ YZ² and Y ∝ Z⁻², show that X ∝ YZ⁶.
Step 1: If Y ∝ Z⁻², then Y = kZ⁻² for some constant k.
Step 2: X ∝ YZ², so X = m(YZ²) for some constant m.
Step 3: Substitute Y: X = m(kZ⁻²)Z² = mkZ⁰ = mk.
Step 4: Thus X is constant, so X ∝ YZ⁶ trivially (as YZ⁶ = kZ⁴ for constant k).
Answer: Shown

cards.title: Partial Variation in Variation
points: Explanation: Partial variation occurs when a quantity is partly constant and partly varies as another quantity. The general formula is y = a + kx, where a is the constant part and kx is the variable part. The graph is a straight line that does not pass through the origin; a is the y-intercept and k is the gradient. Two pairs of values are needed to find a and k. In this section, we solve problems involving partial variation, including real-life examples like cost of production.
Key rule: If y is partly constant and partly varies as x, then y = a + kx.
Key rule: The graph of y = a + kx is a straight line with gradient k and y-intercept a.
Key rule: To find a and k, you need two pairs of (x, y) values and solve simultaneous equations.

cards.title: Partial Variation — Worked Example 9
points: Example: C is partly constant and partly varies as N. C = 45 when N = 10, and C = 87 when N = 24. Find (a) the formula connecting C and N, (b) C when N = 18.
Step 1: C = a + kN, where a and k are constants.
Step 4: Subtract (1) from (2): 42 = 14k → k = 3.
Step 5: Substitute k = 3 into (1): 45 = a + 30 → a = 15.
Step 6: (a) C = 15 + 3N.

cards.title: Partial Variation — Worked Example 10
points: Example: The resistance to motion of a car is partly constant and partly varies as the square of the speed. At 40 km/h the resistance is 530 N, and at 60 km/h it is 730 N. What will be the resistance at 70 km/h?
Step 1: R = a + kV², where a and k are constants.
Step 4: Subtract (1) from (2): 200 = 2000k → k = 1/10.
Step 5: Substitute k = 1/10 into (1): 530 = a + 160 → a = 370.

o-level/form-4/mathematics/Vectors.title: Vectors
snippets: A vector is anything that has both a direction and a size (called its magnitude). A car's velocity is a vector — it has a speed AND a direction. Compare this to something like temperature, which is just a number with no direction: that is called a scalar.
We usually draw a vector as an arrow. The length of the arrow shows the size, and the way it points shows the direction.

If a vector goes from point A to point B, we write it as AB. On squared paper we can also write it as a column vector: the top number is how far across we move, and the bottom number is how far up (or down) we move.
We can do arithmetic with vectors, just like with numbers — but every operation works component by component (top number with top number, bottom with bottom).

cards.title: Naming Vectors and Finding Their Size
points: Definition: A vector is a quantity with both direction and magnitude, usually drawn as an arrow. The length of the arrow is the magnitude; the way it points is the direction.

cards.title: Naming Vectors and Finding Their Size — Worked Example 1
points: Example: A is the point (0, 0) and B is the point (4, 1). Write down the column vector AB, and find its magnitude |AB|.
Step 1: Reading straight from the grid: to get from A to B we move 4 across and 1 up, so AB = (4, 1).
Step 2: The magnitude of a vector is its length, found with Pythagoras' theorem: |AB| = √(4² + 1²).
Answer: |AB| = √17 ≈ 4.12

cards.title: Naming Vectors and Finding Their Size — Worked Example 2
points: Example: Given the vector XY = (-8, 5), find (a) the magnitude |XY|, and (b) the reverse vector YX.
Step 1: Magnitude uses Pythagoras on the two components: |XY| = √((-8)² + 5²) = √(64+25) = √89.
Step 2: The reverse journey YX is simply the negative of XY — same length, opposite direction: YX = -XY = (8, -5).

cards.title: Naming Vectors and Finding Their Size — Worked Example 3
points: Example: A vector p = (3, 4). Find its magnitude |p|.
Step 1: Use Pythagoras directly on the components: |p| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9+16) = √25.
Answer: |p| = 5 — this is the well-known 3-4-5 triangle

cards.title: Multiplying, Adding and Subtracting Vectors — Worked Example 1
points: Example: If p = (-9, 0) and q = (6, -2), find (a) p + q and (b) p - q.
Step 1: Add the top numbers together, then the bottom numbers together: p + q = (-9+6, 0+(-2)).
Step 2: Subtracting works the same way, component by component: p - q = (-9-6, 0-(-2)).
Answer: p + q = (-3, -2) and p - q = (-15, 2)

cards.title: Multiplying, Adding and Subtracting Vectors — Worked Example 2
points: Example: Using Fig 18.2, where AB=(3,-1), BC=(2,1), CD=(-1,4) and DE=(-4,-2): show that DE = -2·BC, and find BC + CD.
Step 1: Multiply BC by -2, component by component: -2 × (2,1) = (-4,-2). This matches DE exactly.
Step 2: Add BC and CD by adding matching components: (2,1) + (-1,4) = (2-1, 1+4).
Answer: DE = -2·BC is confirmed, and BC + CD = (1, 5)

cards.title: Multiplying, Adding and Subtracting Vectors — Worked Example 3
points: Example: If p = (3, 4), find the column vectors 5p and -3p.
Step 1: Multiply every component of p by 5: 5 × (3,4) = (15, 20).
Step 2: Multiply every component of p by -3, remembering the vector will point the opposite way: -3 × (3,4) = (-9, -12).

cards.title: Position Vectors and the Distance Formula
points: Definition: For two points P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂), the vector PQ = (x₂-x₁, y₂-y₁), and the distance |PQ| = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²).

Step 2: Use Pythagoras on the components of PQ: |PQ| = √(8²+6²) = √(64+36) = √100.
Answer: PQ = (8, 6) and |PQ| = 10

cards.title: Proving a Shape Is a Parallelogram — Worked Example 1
points: Example: O(0,0), P(2,2), Q(5,3), R(3,1) are the vertices of quadrilateral OPQR. Show that OPQR is a parallelogram, and find where its diagonals cross.
Step 1: Compute OP = (2,2) and RQ = (5,3)-(3,1) = (2,2). Since OP = RQ, side OP is equal and parallel to side RQ.
Step 2: The diagonals of any parallelogram bisect each other, so the crossing point is the midpoint of OQ: ½(5,3) = (2.5, 1.5).
Answer: OPQR is a parallelogram; the diagonals cross at (2½, 1½)

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Accounting Ratios
snippets: Definition: Mark-up is the percentage of gross profit earned on the cost of sales. It tells you how much profit is added to the cost price to arrive at the selling price.
Mark-up = (Gross Profit / Cost of Sales) × 100

Interpretation: A higher mark-up generally indicates more profit per unit sold, but it can also mean higher prices that may reduce sales volume. Mark-up should be compared with industry averages and past periods to assess pricing strategy and cost control.
Definition: Margin is the percentage of gross profit earned on sales revenue. It shows how much of each sales dollar is left after covering the cost of goods sold.

cards.title: Key Profitability Ratios
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The current ratio measures a business's ability to pay its short-term obligations (due within one year) using its current assets (cash, receivables, inventory, etc.).
Explanation: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities

Explanation: Interpretation: A ratio above 1 indicates the business can cover short-term debts. A very high ratio (e.g., 4:1) might mean excess inventory or cash that could be invested for better returns. A ratio below 1 suggests potential difficulty meeting short-term obligations.
Mark-up: Profit as % of cost
Margin: Profit as % of sales
Net profit %: Net profit as % of sales
Compare over time and with competitors

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Business Ethics
snippets: Business ethics refers to the moral principles and standards that guide behaviour in the business world. In accounting, ethics are the rules and values that govern the conduct of accountants and financial professionals.

Ethics in accounting is essential because financial information is used by many stakeholders—investors, creditors, employees, regulators—to make important decisions. Ethical behaviour ensures that this information is reliable, transparent, and trustworthy.
Ethical behaviour is critical in accounting for several reasons:
Professional accounting bodies (e.g., IFAC, ACCA, AICPA) have established a set of fundamental ethical principles. These principles guide accountants in their daily work and decision-making.

cards.title: Key Points in Business Ethics
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Professional accounting bodies (e.g., IFAC, ACCA, AICPA) have established a set of fundamental ethical principles. These principles guide accountants in their daily work and decision-making.
Explanation: The six core principles are: Professionalism, Integrity, Confidentiality, Competence, Objectivity, and Compliance.
Definition: Professionalism means acting in accordance with the standards of the profession. This includes:
Essential for trust, reputation, and legal compliance
Unethical behaviour can have severe consequences
Maintaining a professional appearance and demeanour.
Adhering to professional standards and best practices.
Acting with courtesy and respect towards colleagues, clients, and the public.

Debentures are a form of long-term loan taken by the company from the public or financial institutions. Debenture holders are creditors of the company, not owners.
Various terms are used to describe the different stages of share capital:
Shareholders' funds represent the total equity belonging to shareholders. It is the residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities.

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Manufacturing Accounts
snippets: Definition: Direct costs are costs that can be directly traced to the production of specific goods. They are part of the prime cost.

Definition: Indirect costs are costs that cannot be directly traced to a specific product. They are also called factory overheads or manufacturing overheads. These costs are incurred in the factory but are not directly part of the product.
Definition: Prime cost is the total of all direct costs. It is the cost that can be directly attributed to the production of goods.
Prime Cost = Direct Materials + Direct Labour + Direct Expenses

points: Explanation: The manufacturing account is used to calculate the cost of production of finished goods. It summarizes all manufacturing costs (direct and indirect) and adjusts for work in progress.

Explanation: After preparing the manufacturing account, the cost of production is transferred to the trading account. The trading account then calculates gross profit by deducting the cost of goods sold from sales.
Explanation: The income statement (trading and profit or loss account) for a manufacturing business follows this structure:
Direct Costs: Traceable to specific products
Indirect Costs: Not traceable; factory overheads
Prime Cost: Direct materials + labour + expenses
WIP adjustment: + opening − closing
Start with raw materials consumed (opening stock + purchases − closing stock).

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Partnerships Formation
snippets: Definition: A partnership is a business relationship between two or more persons (usually 2 to 20, though exceptions exist) who agree to combine their resources (capital, skills, effort) to carry on a business with the aim of sharing profits or losses.
Partnerships are governed by the Partnership Act (e.g., in the UK, the Partnership Act 1890). Unless otherwise agreed, partners share profits and losses equally.

A partnership agreement (or deed) is a written document that sets out the terms and conditions under which the partnership operates. It is not legally required but is highly recommended to avoid disputes.
The income statement (trading and profit or loss account) for a partnership is prepared in the same way as for a sole trader. It calculates the net profit (or loss) for the period.

Explanation: The net profit is then transferred to the appropriation account, where it is divided among the partners according to the partnership agreement.
Explanation: The appropriation account shows how the net profit is distributed among the partners. It includes:

Partnership deed: sets profit-sharing, interest, salaries
Interest on capital: Paid to partners based on their capital balances.
Interest on drawings: Charged to partners for withdrawals; reduces their share.
Partners' salaries: Fixed amounts paid to partners who work in the business.

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Single Entry And Incomplete Records
snippets: Definition: A statement of affairs is a summary of a business's assets and liabilities at a given date. It is used when full double-entry records are not maintained—for example, when the business operates on a single-entry system or when records are incomplete.

The statement of affairs is essentially a balance sheet, but it may be prepared in a simplified format, often with a list of assets on one side and liabilities on the other, or in a vertical format showing net assets.
At the start of the period, if no opening capital figure is given, you can derive it from the opening statement of affairs:
Opening Capital = Total Assets at Start − Total Liabilities at Start

Using the total receivables (debtors) account: By reconciling opening and closing balances with cash received, you can find credit sales.

• Opening & Closing Capital: Calculated as Assets − Liabilities at the respective dates. The change in capital, adjusted for drawings and additional capital, gives net profit.
• Missing Figures: Sales, purchases, expenses, gross profit, net profit, and drawings can all be reconstructed using mark‑up/margin, control accounts, accruals/prepayments, or capital comparison.

• Financial Statements: Once all figures are reconstructed, prepare the income statement and statement of financial position. Always reconcile profit from the income statement with profit from the capital comparison.
• Cash/Bank Summary: A key tool to find missing cash flows and drawings; it links the statement of affairs and income statement.

o-level/form-4/principles-of-accounting/.title: Trial Balance And Errors
snippets: Here is the full picture, side by side — which errors break the trial balance, and which ones slip through it unnoticed.

To work out what an error does to profit, always ask two questions: first, which account was affected — is it a trading account item (sales, purchases, returns, closing stock) that changes gross profit, or an expense/income item that changes net profit? Second, was the figure too high or too low?

Gross profit comes from the trading account, so only these items change it: sales, purchases, returns inwards, returns outwards, carriage inwards, and closing stock (opening stock too, but it is less commonly tested).

Net profit is gross profit minus all other running expenses, plus any other income. So net profit is affected in two ways: anything that changes gross profit automatically changes net profit too, and on top of that, any expense or income account that was recorded wrongly will also change net profit directly.

cards.title: The three steps
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Only four things live inside the trading account: sales, purchases, returns, and closing stock (carriage inwards too, since it is added to purchases). If an error touches any of these, gross profit must be corrected.

Explanation: Once gross profit is corrected, move on to the expense and income accounts (rent, wages, commission received, discounts, depreciation, and so on). Any error here affects net profit only — it does not touch gross profit at all.

Explanation: Examiners usually want the corrections shown in one clear statement, so the marker can see the draft figure, every adjustment, and the final corrected figure — a simple before-and-after comparison. Watch below as each line is handwritten into the exam book step by step:

Decide whether the account is a trading account item (changes gross profit) or an expense/income item (changes net profit only).
Work out whether the correction should be added to profit (because profit was too low) or subtracted from profit (because profit was too high).

cards.title: 🎉 Key Takeaways
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Effect of Errors: Some errors break the trial balance (e.g. single entry, casting errors); others don't (omission, commission, principle, original entry, reversal, compensating errors) — and a balanced trial balance never proves the books are fully correct.

• Adjustments: Trading account items (sales, purchases, returns, stock) adjust gross profit; expense and income items adjust net profit only — always compare the correct figure against the recorded figure to know whether to add or subtract.

• Revised Statement of Profit: Show corrections as a reconciliation (draft → adjustments → corrected) or redraw the full trading and profit or loss account — both must reach the same corrected net profit.

• Revised Statement of Financial Position: Trace each profit correction to its matching asset, liability, or capital, present only the affected sections as an extract, and confirm assets still equal capital plus liabilities.

polytechnic/banking-nc/customer-accounts.title: The Art of Customer Inquiries
snippets: Master the art of communication in banking, from building trust and handling inquiries to professional ethics and the 5 C's of communication.

Banking isn't just about numbers and transactions; it's fundamentally about trust. Money is a very personal and often emotional topic for people. Good communication is the bridge we use to build that trust. When a customer knows they can ask a question and get a clear, respectful, and helpful answer, they develop loyalty to the bank.

Therefore, learning how to communicate effectively is not just a "soft skill"—it is the single most important tool you will use every day as a banking professional. It prevents errors, solves problems, builds the bank's reputation, and makes your job more effective and rewarding. It is the foundation upon which all other banking skills are built.
Good communication is the lifeblood of customer service in banking. Here are ten specific reasons why it is so important when handling customer inquiries:
