cards.title: Polynomial Functions, Indices & Logarithms
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Evaluating a polynomial like at a given value of x by substituting directly means computing four separate powers. Horner's method avoids this by rewriting the polynomial as nested multiplications — you only ever multiply by x, never raise x to a power. This is faster, has fewer steps, and produces fewer rounding errors. It is also the basis of synthetic division. The key insight: work from the highest-degree coefficient inward, alternating multiply-then-add.
Explanation: Rewrite as nested multiplications to minimise computation and rounding errors.

Explanation: When you divide a polynomial by a linear expression like, you get a quotient and a remainder. The Remainder Theorem says you do not need to perform the full division to find that remainder — just substitute into the polynomial and evaluate it. That result is the remainder. This saves a huge amount of working, especially for higher-degree polynomials.
Start with the coefficient of the highest power (aₙ).
Multiply by the substitution value c.
Repeat until you add the constant term (a₀).
• Move decimal until one non-zero digit is on the left.
• Count moves: left → n is positive; right → n is negative.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Numbers & Algebra – Understand number sets, rounding, base conversions, BODMAS, equations, transposition, factorisation, quadratic equations, and function notation.

cards.title: Mass, Specific Gravity & Relative Density
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Mass is a fundamental property of an object that measures its resistance to acceleration. It is often described as the amount of "stuff" or matter an object contains.
Definition: SI Unit: The standard SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). Other common units include grams (g) and pounds (lbs).

Definition: Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance. Usually, the reference substance is water at 4°C, which has a density of approximately 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.
Formula: Specific Gravity = (Density of substance) / (Density of water)
Formula: Relative Density = (Density of substance) / (Density of reference substance)
Mass is an intrinsic property of an object and remains constant regardless of its location.
Mass is different from weight. Weight is the force exerted on an object by gravity, while mass is the amount of matter in the object.
Specific gravity is a dimensionless quantity (it has no units).

SI Unit: The standard SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). Other common units include grams (g) and pounds (lbs).

Definition: Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance. Usually, the reference substance is water at 4°C, which has a density of approximately 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.
Specific Gravity = (Density of substance) / (Density of water)

blocks.title: Key points about Mass, Specific Gravity & Relative Density
items: Mass is an intrinsic property of an object and remains constant regardless of its location.
Mass is different from weight. Weight is the force exerted on an object by gravity, while mass is the amount of matter in the object.
Specific gravity is a dimensionless quantity (it has no units).
If the specific gravity of a substance is greater than 1, it is denser than water and will sink. If it is less than 1, it is less dense than water and will float.
Relative density is also a dimensionless quantity.

In many contexts, "relative density" and "specific gravity" are used interchangeably. When the reference substance is water, the numerical values of specific gravity and relative density are identical.

cards.title: Resolving Forces Using Trigonometry
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: A force acting at an angle can be split into a horizontal component and a vertical component.
Definition: Where F is the magnitude of the force and θ is the angle between the force and the horizontal axis.
Explanation: Both Fx and Fy are positive because the force is in the first quadrant.
Formula: Fx = F × cos(θ) [Horizontal Component]
Formula: Fy = F × sin(θ) [Vertical Component]

cards.title: Stress (Normal or Direct)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Stress (normal or direct) is the internal resistance offered by a material to an externally applied force per unit area.
Explanation: SI Units: Pascal (Pa) = N/m². Common units: MPa, kPa, psi.
Explanation: Example: Steel rod, area = 0.001 m², force = 10,000 N
Formula: Stress (σ) = Force (F) / Area (A)

cards.title: Direct strain (ε)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Direct strain (ε) is the measure of deformation of a material when subjected to a force. It is a dimensionless quantity.
Explanation: Strain is dimensionless — it represents the amount of deformation per unit length.
Explanation: Example: 2-metre metal bar stretched by 2 mm
Formula: ε = ΔL / L (change in length / original length)
Formula: ε = 0.002 m / 2 m = 0.001 (dimensionless)

cards.title: Morse Test Procedure
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The Morse test is a method used to determine the indicated power (IP) of a multi-cylinder internal combustion engine.
Explanation: BP (all) = 40 kW | Cut 1: 30 kW | Cut 2: 31 kW | Cut 3: 32 kW | Cut 4: 33 kW
Formula: IP (cylinder) = BP (all cylinders) − BP (cylinder cut out)
Formula: IP cyl1 = 40−30=10 kW | IP cyl2 = 40−31=9 kW

Explanation: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain.
Explanation: The modulus of elasticity. E = Stress / Strain.

cards.title: Gearbox, Steering Box & Final Drive Ratios
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: A car has a gearbox ratio of 3:1 in first gear and a final drive ratio of 4:1. If the engine is turning at 3000 RPM, what is the speed of the drive wheels?
Explanation: Answer: Drive wheels rotate at 250 RPM.
Formula: Overall Ratio = 3 × 4 = 12:1
Formula: Drive Wheel Speed = 3000 RPM / 12 = 250 RPM

points: Definition: i) Nominal Value (E12 Series): The nominal value is the intended or designated resistance of a resistor, measured in ohms (Ω).

Definition: E12 Series: This is a standard series of preferred resistor values. It provides a logarithmic progression of values within each decade (e.g., 10-100 Ω, 100-1000 Ω). The E12 series has 12 values per decade, which are: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. To get other values you multiply those values by powers of 10. For example, 100, 120, 150, 180, 220, 270, 330, 390, 470, 560, 680, 820. Symbol: Ω (Ohm)

Explanation: ii) Power Rating: The power rating indicates the maximum amount of power (in watts, W) that a resistor can safely dissipate as heat without being damaged. cards.title: Electrostatic Principles in Electrical & Electronics Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: 1. Electric Charge: Everything is made of atoms, which have positive (protons), negative (electrons), and neutral (neutrons) parts. Usually, things have the same number of positive and negative parts, so they are neutral. But sometimes electrons can move, making something have more or less negative charge. This imbalance creates an electric charge. Objects can become charged by rubbing them together (transferring electrons). Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. Charge measured in Coulombs (C).

Explanation: 2. Coulomb's Law: F = k * (q1 * q2) / r², where k = 8.99×10⁹ N m²/C². Force is directly proportional to product of charges, inversely proportional to square of distance. If you double one charge, force doubles; if you double distance, force becomes one quarter.

Definition: 3. Electric Fields: Region around a charged object where another charged object feels a force. Field lines go from positive to negative. Strength shown by line density. Electric field E = F/q. Direction is the force on a positive test charge.

cards.title: Passive Components in Electrical & Electronics Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Passive components are electronic components that do not require an external power source to operate.
They cannot amplify or generate electrical signals. Instead, they either dissipate, store, or release energy.
They do not provide gain or amplification.
They can control the flow of current and voltage.
They can store or dissipate energy.
Examples include resistors, capacitors, and inductors.

cards.title: Resistors as Passive Components
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Resistors oppose the flow of electrical current.
They convert electrical energy into heat, which is then dissipated, meaning it is released or dispersed into the surrounding environment, typically as thermal energy.
Resistors do not generate their own electrical signals.
They do not amplify or increase the power of a signal.
They simply resist the flow of current, causing a voltage drop and dissipating power as heat.
They do not require an external power source to function.

cards.title: Dielectrics in Electrical & Electronics Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: What are Dielectrics? Insulating materials that can be polarized when an electric field is applied. They store electrical energy by rearranging internal charges.
Non-Polar: Molecules have evenly distributed charges (air, benzene, paraffin). Induced dipoles when field applied.
Polar: Molecules have permanent dipole moment (water, alcohol). Dipoles align with field.
Linear: Polarization ∝ electric field (predictable).
Non-Linear: Polarization not proportional to field; may exhibit hysteresis (ferroelectric materials like barium titanate, PZT).
Ferroelectric: Spontaneous polarization that can be reversed; used in capacitors, sensors, memory devices.

cards.title: Resistor Faults in Electrical & Electronics Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Factors Contributing to Resistor Faults: Overheating (exceeding power rating), environmental factors (moisture, humidity, temperature variations), physical stress (impact, vibration), electrical stress (voltage surges, excessive current), manufacturing defects, aging.

1. Open: Complete break, infinite resistance. Causes: overstress from excessive current or voltage, physical damage, thermal stress, manufacturing defects. Effects: circuit interrupted, current flow stops.
2. Increased Resistance: Value increases beyond tolerance. Causes: overheating, aging, moisture ingress, damage from voltage surges. Effects: degraded performance, wrong voltage output.
3. Decreased Resistance: Value decreases below tolerance. Rare, due to certain types of electrical overstress. Effects: increased current flow, potential damage to other components.
4. Short: Resistance near zero. Causes: severe electrical overstress, physical damage. Effects: excessive current, damage, fire hazard.

cards.title: Non-Linear Resistors in Electrical & Electronics Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Non-linear resistors are components where the resistance changes in a non-proportional way with variations in voltage, temperature, or light. This contrasts with linear resistors, which maintain a constant resistance.

Explanation: ii) Voltage Dependent Resistors (VDRs) or Varistors: Their resistance changes significantly with applied voltage. At low voltages, high resistance; at high voltages, resistance drops sharply. Used for surge protection. Applications: Protecting electronic circuits from voltage spikes and surges, such as those caused by lightning or power line fluctuations; used in power supplies, telecommunications equipment, and automotive electronics.

Explanation: iii) Light Dependent Resistors (LDRs) or Photoresistors: Their resistance changes with light intensity. In darkness, high resistance; in bright light, resistance decreases. Used for light sensing and control. Applications: Automatic lighting control (streetlights, security lights); light detection in cameras and light meters; alarm systems and optical switches.

snippets: Energy band theory, PN junctions, diodes, rectification, transistors, optoelectronics, and integrated circuits.
In electronic materials, conduction is explained using energy band theory, which describes how electrons behave in different energy levels. The two main bands are:
A PN junction is formed when a p-type semiconductor and an n-type semiconductor are joined together. This junction is the basic structure of diodes, transistors, and many other semiconductor devices.
Example Applications: Diodes (one‑way current), Solar cells (light to electricity).

cards.title: Formation of a PN Junction
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: A PN junction is formed when a p-type semiconductor and an n-type semiconductor are joined together. This junction is the basic structure of diodes, transistors, and many other semiconductor devices.
Explanation: Example Applications: Diodes (one‑way current), Solar cells (light to electricity).
Bringing P-type and N-type together – Electrons diffuse from n-region to p-region, holes diffuse from p-region to n-region.
Formation of the Depletion Region – Recombination leaves immobile ions, creating a zone with no free charge carriers.
Formation of the Built-in Electric Field – Immobile ions create an electric field from n-side to p-side, preventing further diffusion.
Equilibrium Condition – Diffusion is balanced by the electric field, resulting in a stable built-in potential (≈0.7V for Si, 0.3V for Ge).

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Occurs in pure semiconductors (e.g., silicon, germanium).
At room temperature or higher, some electrons in the valence band absorb thermal energy and jump to the conduction band, creating electron-hole pairs.
The number of free electrons equals the number of holes.
Conductivity depends on temperature and the material's intrinsic properties.
Occurs in doped semiconductors, where impurities are added to increase conductivity.
Two types: n-type semiconductor: Doped with a pentavalent element (e.g., phosphorus in silicon), providing extra electrons. Majority carriers = electrons.

cards.title: Effect of Thermal Agitation and Light on Conductivity
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: As temperature increases, more electrons gain energy to cross the band gap, increasing conductivity.
In intrinsic semiconductors, higher temperatures generate more electron-hole pairs.
In extrinsic semiconductors, too much heat can ionize dopant atoms, potentially reducing controlled conductivity.
Photoconductivity: When light with energy equal to or greater than the band gap hits a semiconductor, electrons absorb photons and jump to the conduction band.
This principle is used in photoresistors, solar cells, and photodiodes.
More light → More free electrons and holes → Increased conductivity.

cards.title: Formation of Potential Barrier and Depletion Layer in an Unbiased PN Junction

Potential Barrier: Electric potential that prevents further movement of carriers (≈0.7V for Si, 0.3V for Ge).
Thickness depends on doping – higher doping = thinner depletion layer.
Higher temperature increases carrier generation, slightly reducing the barrier.

cards.title: Effect of Minority Charge Carriers on Blocking Current in Reverse Bias
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details

In reverse bias, these minority carriers move towards the terminals, creating a small reverse saturation current (I s ).
Temperature increases minority carriers → higher leakage current.
At very high reverse voltage: Zener breakdown (heavily doped, low voltage) or Avalanche breakdown (lightly doped, high voltage).

cards.title: Experiment with a Darlington Transistor as a Switching Amplifier

points: Definition: A Darlington transistor is a pair of transistors connected together to form a single device with high current gain. This configuration is used in switching applications to amplify weak signals.

Explanation: Power supply provides voltage. Load resistor limits current through LED/motor. Darlington transistor base receives small current from switch via R B. When switch closed, base current turns transistor ON, allowing large collector current to flow through load.
Explanation: Operation: Switch open → no base current → OFF → load off. Switch closed → small base current → high collector current → load on.

polytechnic/nc-auto/electronic-fuel-inje.title: Fuel Injection System Inspection
snippets: Complete guide to fuel injection system safety, electronic aspects, operation, components, sensors, actuators, ECU identification, and diagnostics.

The ECU is the "brain" of the fuel injection system. It receives input from the sensors, processes the data, and controls the fuel injectors and other actuators. It uses pre-programmed maps and adaptive learning to optimise fuel delivery for various driving conditions.
The fuel pump draws fuel from the fuel tank and sends it through a fuel filter to the fuel rail. The fuel rail distributes fuel to the individual fuel injectors.
Air enters the engine through the air intake system, passing through an air filter and the throttle body. Sensors measure the amount of air entering the engine.

cards.title: Electronic Control Unit (ECU)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: The ECU is the "brain" of the fuel injection system. It receives input from the sensors, processes the data, and controls the fuel injectors and other actuators. It uses pre-programmed maps and adaptive learning to optimise fuel delivery for various driving conditions.

cards.title: Fuel Handling in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Ventilation: Work in a well-ventilated area to prevent accumulation of flammable fuel vapours.
No Smoking/Open Flames: Absolutely no smoking or open flames near the fuel system. Fuel is highly flammable.
Fuel Spills: Clean up any fuel spills immediately with absorbent materials. Dispose of them properly.

Pressure Relief: Before disconnecting any fuel lines, relieve the fuel pressure in the system. Follow the manufacturer's instructions. Often done by removing the fuel pump fuse and trying to start the car to use up the fuel in the fuel rail.
Eye Protection: Wear safety glasses to protect your eyes from fuel spray.
Skin Protection: Wear nitrile gloves to protect your skin from fuel, which can be irritating and harmful.

cards.title: Fuel System Components (Mechanical / Electro-Mechanical)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Fuel Accumulator: Maintains residual fuel pressure after engine shut-off. Helps prevent vapour lock and ensures quick restarts.
Fuel Filter: Removes contaminants from fuel, protecting injectors and other components.
Primary Pressure Regulator: Maintains constant fuel pressure in the fuel rail. Ensures consistent fuel delivery to injectors.
Air-Flow Sensor (Air-Flow Meter): In mechanical systems (e.g., K-Jetronic), a mechanical flap that moves in response to airflow. Its movement controls the fuel distributor.
Fuel Distributor: In mechanical systems, distributes fuel to individual injectors based on air-flow sensor position. Divides fuel flow into equal portions.
Differential Pressure Valves: Maintain a constant pressure difference across the fuel metering slits in the fuel distributor. Ensures correct fuel delivery.

cards.title: Electrical Safety in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Battery Disconnect: Disconnect the vehicle's battery (negative terminal first) before working on any electrical components of the fuel injection system. Prevents accidental shorts and electrical damage.
Proper Tools: Use insulated tools when working on electrical components.
Component Handling: Handle electronic components carefully to avoid static discharge, which can damage them.
High Pressure: Fuel injection systems operate at high pressure. Never loosen or disconnect fuel lines while the system is pressurised.
Hot Engine: Do not work on the fuel system when the engine is hot. Allow it to cool down to prevent burns.

cards.title: Sensors in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Mass Airflow (MAF) Sensor / Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) Sensor: Measures the amount of air entering the engine.
Oxygen (O₂) Sensor: Monitors the oxygen content in the exhaust gases, providing feedback for fuel mixture adjustments.
Throttle Position Sensor (TPS): Detects the position of the throttle plate, indicating the driver's demand for power.
Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) Sensor: Measures the engine's temperature, influencing fuel mixture and timing.
Crankshaft Position Sensor (CKP) and Camshaft Position Sensor (CMP): Provide information about the engine's rotational speed and position.

cards.title: Fuel Injection System Inspection: What to Remember
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Safety Precautions – Work in ventilated areas, avoid flames, relieve fuel pressure, wear PPE, disconnect battery, handle electronics carefully, and keep a fire extinguisher ready.

• Electronic Aspects – Sensors (MAF/MAP, O₂, TPS, ECT, CKP/CMP), ECU (processing, memory, communication), Actuators (injectors, fuel pump, IAC), and Diagnostics (OBD-II, scan tools, wiring inspection).
• System Operation – Six-step process: Fuel Delivery, Air Intake, Fuel Injection, Combustion, Exhaust, and Feedback Loop (closed-loop control).

• Components – Sensors (MAF, MAP, O₂, ECT, CKP, CMP), Actuators (injectors, fuel pump, stepper motor), Mechanical components (accumulator, filter, regulator, distributor, warm‑up regulator, cold‑start valve, auxiliary air device), and adjustments (idle mixture, idle speed, throttle valve).

• ECU Identifying – Follow safety protocols, understand ECU computer operation (processing, memory, communication, software), recognise input sensors and output actuators, and appreciate the difference between older mechanical and modern electronic systems.

cards.title: Sensors in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Mass Airflow (MAF) Sensor / Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) Sensor: MAF measures the mass of air entering the engine (hot-wire/hot film). MAP measures pressure in the intake manifold to calculate air density. Critical for correct air/fuel ratio.
Oxygen (O₂) Sensor: Monitors oxygen content in exhaust. Provides feedback for closed-loop fuel control, allowing precise air/fuel mixture adjustments.
Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) Sensor: Measures coolant temperature. Influences fuel mixture, ignition timing, and other engine parameters.

Crankshaft Position Sensor (CKP) and Camshaft Position Sensor (CMP): CKP determines crankshaft position and engine speed. CMP determines camshaft position (valve position). Essential for accurate fuel injection and ignition timing.

cards.title: Computer Operation in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Processing Power: ECUs contain microprocessors that process data from sensors and execute control algorithms. Processing power determines ability to handle complex calculations and real-time control.
Memory: ECUs have memory to store program data, sensor readings, and diagnostic information. Types: ROM (Read-Only Memory), RAM (Random Access Memory), or flash memory.

Communication: ECUs communicate with other vehicle systems and diagnostic tools through protocols like CAN (Controller Area Network), OBD-II (On-Board Diagnostics II), and others. Understanding these is vital for diagnostics and reprogramming.
Software: The software loaded onto the ECU dictates how the car operates. Calibrated by vehicle manufacturers and sometimes aftermarket companies.

Idle Air Control (IAC) Valve / Electronic Throttle Control: Controls the amount of air bypassing the throttle plate at idle.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: The ECU determines the appropriate amount of fuel to inject based on sensor data.
The ECU sends electrical pulses to the fuel injectors, causing them to open and spray fuel into the intake manifold or cylinders.
The length of the electrical pulse (pulse width) determines the amount of fuel injected.

cards.title: Safety Precautions in Fuel Injection System Inspection
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Electrical Safety: Always disconnect the vehicle's battery (negative terminal first) before working on any ECU or related wiring. Prevents accidental shorts and potential damage to sensitive electronics. Use proper grounding techniques to avoid static discharge. Be aware of potential voltage spikes when disconnecting or connecting components.
Component Handling: ECUs are delicate electronic devices. Handle with care to avoid physical damage. Avoid exposing the ECU to extreme temperatures, moisture, or strong magnetic fields.

Software Safety: When using diagnostic tools or reprogramming the ECU, ensure reliable and compatible software. Incorrect software can cause serious damage. Always back up any existing ECU data before making changes.

cards.title: Intermittent Injection Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Fuel is injected in pulses, timed to coincide with the engine's intake stroke. This allows for more precise fuel control and better fuel economy.
L-Jetronic: An electronic, multi-point fuel injection system. Uses a mass airflow (MAF) sensor to measure intake air volume. Electronically controlled injectors deliver fuel intermittently.
LE-Jetronic: A simplified version of the L-Jetronic system.
LH-Jetronic: Uses a hot-wire MAF sensor for more accurate air measurement.
LU-Jetronic: A less common variation with variations in the sensors used.
Motronic: A combined fuel injection and ignition control system. Integrates fuel injection, ignition timing, and other engine management functions. Available in many variations.
Mono-Jetronic: A single-point fuel injection system (throttle body injection). Uses a single injector located in the throttle body. Simpler and less expensive than multi-point systems.

cards.title: Common Faults in Fuel Injection System Layout & Diagnostics
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Fuel Pump Failure: Worn pump, electrical issues, contaminated fuel. Symptoms: No fuel delivery, low fuel pressure, engine stalling.
Clogged Fuel Filter: Contaminated fuel. Symptoms: Low fuel pressure, poor engine performance, engine stalling.
Faulty Fuel Injectors: Clogged injectors, electrical failures, worn seals. Symptoms: Misfires, poor idle, reduced power, increased fuel consumption.
Faulty Sensors: Electrical failures, contamination, wear and tear. Symptoms: Poor engine performance, increased emissions, inaccurate sensor readings.
Wiring and Connection Problems: Corrosion, damage, loose connections. Symptoms: Intermittent problems, sensor failures, actuator failures.
Vacuum Leaks: Cracked hoses, bad gaskets. Symptoms: Poor idle, increased fuel consumption, rough running.

cards.title: Machines and Equipment
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Scan Tools (Diagnostic Scanners): Handheld or laptop-based devices that connect to the OBD-II port. Used to read DTCs, monitor live data, perform actuator tests, and reprogram ECUs. Vary in complexity from basic code readers to advanced professional-grade scanners.
Oscilloscopes: Used to visualise electrical signals from sensors and actuators. Helpful for diagnosing intermittent problems and analysing signal patterns.
Multimeters: Essential for checking voltage, resistance, and continuity in electrical circuits.
Fuel Pressure Testers: Used to measure fuel pressure in the fuel rail.
Fuel Injector Testers: Used to test the function of the fuel injectors.
Laptop/PC: For running advanced diagnostic software, accessing online repair information, and reprogramming ECUs.

cards.title: Differences in Fuel Injection System Layout & Diagnostics
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Mechanical systems (like K-Jetronic) rely on mechanical components and fuel pressure.
Electronic systems (like L-Jetronic, Motronic, and GDI) use sensors, ECUs, and electrically controlled injectors.
Continuous injection systems deliver fuel constantly, while intermittent systems deliver fuel in pulses.
Direct injection injects fuel directly into the cylinder, and indirect injection injects fuel into the intake manifold.

cards.title: Fuel Pressure Test
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Connect a fuel pressure gauge to the fuel rail.
Check the fuel pressure against the manufacturer's specifications.
Observe if the pressure holds steady or drops.
This checks the fuel pump, pressure regulator, and fuel lines.

cards.title: Fuel Injector Testing
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Pulse Testing: Use a noid light or oscilloscope to check for electrical pulses to the injectors. Verifies the ECU's control of the injectors.
Resistance Testing: Use a multimeter to check the resistance of the injector coils. Identifies open or shorted injectors.
Spray Pattern Testing: Remove the injectors and observe the spray pattern. A good injector will have a fine, even mist.
Volume Testing: Measure the amount of fuel each injector delivers over a set amount of time.

cards.title: Fault Codes (Diagnostic Trouble Codes - DTCs)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Codes generated by the ECU when it detects a problem with the fuel injection system or other vehicle systems.
Each DTC corresponds to a specific fault, such as a faulty sensor, actuator, or wiring issue.
Scan tools are used to read and interpret DTCs.
DTCs provide a starting point for diagnosis, but further testing is often required to pinpoint the exact cause of the problem.

cards.title: Oxygen Sensor (Same as Lambda Sensor)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Terminology: "Lambda sensor" and "oxygen sensor" are generally used interchangeably.
Explanation: Location: Typically located in the exhaust manifold before and/or after the catalytic converter.
Explanation: Function: The sensor before the catalytic converter provides feedback for air/fuel ratio control. The sensor after the catalytic converter monitors the catalytic converter's efficiency.
Zirconia sensors: Generate a voltage signal based on the oxygen difference between the exhaust gas and ambient air.
Titania sensors: Change electrical resistance based on oxygen content.
Wideband sensors: Provides a more accurate and linear output over a wider range of air/fuel ratios. Used in more modern vehicles.

cards.title: Catalytic Converters in Emissions Control Components & Principles
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Work in conjunction with the oxygen sensors to convert harmful exhaust gases into less harmful substances. They use precious metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium) as catalysts. They reduce CO, HC, and NOx emissions.

Explanation: Function: Catalytic converters are devices within the exhaust system that convert harmful pollutants into less harmful substances. They use precious metals (platinum, palladium, and rhodium) as catalysts to facilitate chemical reactions.
Explanation: Importance: Significantly reduce harmful emissions, helping to meet environmental regulations. They are a vital component of modern emission control systems.
Oxidation: Platinum and palladium catalyze the oxidation of carbon monoxide (CO) to carbon dioxide (CO₂) and hydrocarbons (HC) to CO₂ and water (H₂O).
Reduction: Rhodium catalyzes the reduction of nitrogen oxides (NOx) to nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂).
Three-way catalytic converters: Used in gasoline engines, they perform all three reactions (oxidation and reduction).
Two-way catalytic converters: Older type, that only oxidised HC and CO.

cards.title: Common Faults/Codes (DTCs)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) are the language of modern vehicle diagnostics. They are generated by the vehicle's onboard computer system when it detects a malfunction. Understanding these codes is essential for efficient troubleshooting.

OBD-II Standardisation: The OBD-II (On-Board Diagnostics II) standard has created a uniform system for accessing and interpreting these codes, making it easier for technicians to diagnose problems across different vehicle makes and models.

Code Structure: DTCs follow a specific format, which reveals information about the affected vehicle system. For example: The first character (letter) indicates the system (P for Powertrain, B for Body, C for Chassis, U for Network). The subsequent digits provide more specific details about the fault.
Common Fault Areas: Engine Misfires (P0300 series): Often related to ignition, fuel, or compression issues.
Oxygen Sensor Problems (P01xx series): Indicate issues with the oxygen sensors, which are crucial for emissions control.
Mass Airflow (MAF) Sensor Issues (P0100 series): Affect the engine's ability to measure incoming air.

snippets: Complete guide to construction, operation, care and maintenance, safety precautions, battery ratings (Ah, RC, CCA), testing instruments, and charging methods.

Discharging: During discharge, a chemical reaction occurs where lead dioxide and sponge lead react with sulfuric acid, forming lead sulphate (PbSO₄) on both plates. This process releases electrons, providing electrical current.

Charging: During charging, an external electrical source reverses the chemical reaction, converting lead sulphate back to lead dioxide and sponge lead, and restoring the sulfuric acid concentration in the electrolyte.
Discharging: During discharge, a chemical reaction occurs where nickel hydroxide and cadmium react with potassium hydroxide, releasing electrons.

cards.title: Ampere-Hour Capacity (Ah)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Ampere-hour capacity is a measure of a battery's ability to deliver a specific amount of current over a period of time. It indicates how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Explanation: A battery with a higher Ah rating can supply more current for a longer duration than a battery with a lower Ah rating. For example, a 100Ah battery can theoretically deliver 100 amperes for one hour, or 50 amperes for two hours, and so on. However, the actual capacity can vary depending on factors like temperature, discharge rate, and battery age.
Explanation: Formula (General Concept): Ah = Current (A) × Time (h)

cards.title: Hydrometer in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: A hydrometer consists of a glass tube with a weighted bulb at the bottom and a graduated scale inside.

Definition: Operating Principle: It measures the specific gravity of the battery's electrolyte. Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of the electrolyte to the density of water. The specific gravity of the electrolyte is directly related to the state of charge of a lead-acid battery.
Explanation: Interpretation: A higher specific gravity indicates a higher state of charge.
Insert the hydrometer's nozzle into the battery's cell.
Draw electrolyte into the tube until the float rises freely.
Read the specific gravity on the graduated scale at the liquid level.
Compare the reading to the manufacturer's specifications to determine the battery's state of charge.

cards.title: Reserve Capacity (RC)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Reserve capacity is the amount of time (in minutes) a fully charged battery can deliver 25 amperes at 80°F (26.7°C) before its voltage drops below 10.5 volts.

Explanation: This rating is particularly important for automotive batteries. It indicates how long a vehicle can operate on battery power alone if the charging system fails. It essentially provides a "backup" time for essential electrical systems.
Explanation: Formula: There isn't a simple calculation formula. Reserve capacity is determined through standardised testing.

cards.title: Cold Cranking Amps (CCA)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Cold cranking amps is a measure of a battery's ability to deliver a high current at low temperatures. It's the number of amperes a battery can deliver at 0°F (-17.8°C) for 30 seconds while maintaining a voltage of 7.2 volts or higher.

Explanation: This rating is crucial for starting a vehicle in cold weather. Cold temperatures reduce battery performance, and a high CCA rating ensures the battery can provide enough power to crank the engine.
Explanation: Formula: Similar to reserve capacity, CCA is determined through standardised testing rather than a direct calculation.

cards.title: Care and Maintenance
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Electrolyte Level: Regularly check the electrolyte level and add distilled water as needed. Low electrolyte can damage the plates.
Clean Terminals: Keep terminals clean and free from corrosion. Use a wire brush and apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly or battery terminal protector.
Charge Regularly: Avoid deep discharges, as they can shorten battery life. Regularly charge the battery to maintain its capacity.
Avoid Extreme Temperatures: Extreme temperatures can affect battery performance and lifespan.
Proper Ventilation: Ensure adequate ventilation when charging to prevent the build-up of explosive hydrogen gas.
Specific Gravity: The specific gravity of the electrolyte can be measured to determine the state of charge.

cards.title: Care and Maintenance
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Avoid Deep Discharges (Memory Effect): Ni-Cd batteries can develop a "memory effect" if repeatedly discharged to the same level. This reduces their capacity. Avoid partial discharges when possible. When needed, fully discharge, and then recharge the battery.
Charge Regularly: Regular charging is essential to maintain battery health.
Avoid Overcharging: Overcharging can damage the battery. Use a charger designed for Ni-Cd batteries.
Proper Ventilation: Ensure adequate ventilation when charging to prevent the build-up of gases.
Storage: Store Ni-Cd batteries in a cool, dry place.
Dispose of Properly: Ni-Cd batteries contain cadmium, which is a toxic heavy metal. Dispose of them according to local regulations.

cards.title: Acids (Electrolyte) in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Protective Gear: Wear appropriate PPE, including safety glasses, gloves, and an apron, when handling battery acid.
Avoid Contact: Prevent acid from contacting skin, eyes, or clothing.
Eye Wash and First Aid: Have an eye wash station and first aid kit readily available.
Dilution: Always add acid to water, never water to acid, to prevent splashing and heat generation.
Neutralisation: Use baking soda to neutralise acid spills.
Proper Disposal: Dispose of used acid and contaminated materials according to local regulations.

cards.title: High-Rate Discharge Tester
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: A high-rate discharge tester consists of a heavy-duty resistor, an ammeter, and a voltmeter.
Explanation: Operating Principle: It applies a high current load to the battery for a short period, simulating the load of starting an engine. The voltmeter measures the battery's voltage under load.
Explanation: Interpretation: A significant voltage drop indicates a weak or failing battery.
Connect the tester's leads to the battery terminals, observing correct polarity.
Apply the load for a specified time (e.g., 15 seconds).
Observe the voltmeter reading during the test.
Compare the voltage reading to the manufacturer's specifications to determine the battery's condition.

cards.title: Cadmium Tester in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: A cadmium tester consists of a voltmeter and a cadmium electrode.

Explanation: Operating Principle: It measures the voltage between the cadmium electrode and the positive and negative plates of a nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd) battery. This allows for the individual checking of the positive and negative plates.
Explanation: Interpretation: A reading outside the specified range indicates a faulty plate.
Carefully expose the electrolyte of the Ni-Cd battery.
Insert the cadmium electrode and the voltmeter probes into the electrolyte, making contact with the appropriate plates.
Compare the readings to the manufacturer's specifications to determine the condition of the individual plates.

cards.title: Constant Current Charging
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Principle: The charger delivers a constant current to the battery, regardless of the battery's voltage.
Explanation: Application: Suitable for charging Ni-Cd batteries and some lead-acid batteries.
Connect the charger to the battery, observing correct polarity.
Set the charger to the desired current level.
Monitor the battery's voltage and temperature during charging.
Terminate charging when the battery reaches the desired voltage or when the charging current drops to a low level.

cards.title: Constant Voltage Charging
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Principle: The charger maintains a constant voltage across the battery terminals, allowing the charging current to decrease as the battery charges.
Explanation: Application: Commonly used for charging lead-acid batteries.
Connect the charger to the battery, observing correct polarity.
Set the charger to the desired voltage level.
Monitor the charging current, which will decrease as the battery charges.
Terminate charging when the charging current reaches a low level.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Principle: A controlled overcharge used to balance the charge between the cells of a lead-acid battery.
Explanation: Application: Used periodically to maintain the health of lead-acid batteries in standby power applications.
Explanation: End of Learning Outcome 1 — Batteries: Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium

Apply a higher-than-normal voltage for a specific period.
Monitor the battery's voltage and temperature.

cards.title: Battery Charging in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Ventilation: Batteries release hydrogen gas during charging, which is highly explosive. Charge batteries in a well-ventilated area to prevent gas build-up. Avoid enclosed spaces like closets or small rooms.

Proper Connections: Ensure the charger is properly connected to the battery terminals, observing correct polarity (+ to + and - to -). Incorrect connections can cause sparks, explosions, or damage to the battery or charger.
Charger Settings: Use a charger with appropriate voltage and current settings for the battery type (lead-acid, Ni-Cd, etc.). Overcharging can overheat and damage the battery.
No Smoking or Open Flames: Keep sparks, flames, and smoking materials away from batteries during charging.
Disconnecting: Turn off the charger before disconnecting the battery. Disconnect the negative terminal first, then the positive terminal.

cards.title: Battery Storage in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Cool, Dry Place: Store batteries in a cool, dry place to prevent corrosion and self discharge.
Upright Position: Store lead-acid batteries in an upright position to prevent electrolyte leakage.
Separate Storage: Store different battery types separately to avoid chemical reactions. Store away from flammable materials.
Regular Checks: Periodically check stored batteries for voltage and electrolyte levels (if applicable).
Neutralisation: Keep a neutralising agent, such as baking soda, nearby in case of acid spills.

Explanation: Application: Can help to reduce sulfation in lead-acid batteries.

Allow the charger to cycle through its pulse and rest periods.
Monitor the battery's voltage and temperature.

cards.title: Construction in Batteries — Lead-Acid & Nickel-Cadmium
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Consists of positive plates made of lead dioxide (PbO₂) and negative plates made of sponge lead (Pb).
These plates are immersed in an electrolyte, which is a solution of sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and water.
The plates are separated by insulators to prevent short circuits.
The battery is housed in a durable plastic case.

polytechnic/nc-auto/ignition-starting-ch.title: Ignition System — Components, Operation & Diagnosis
snippets: Complete guide to conventional ignition, triggering methods, electronic ignition systems (DIS, direct ignition, CDI, energy transfer), spark plugs, heat ranges, and fault diagnosis.
Purpose: A ballast resistor is used to limit the current flowing through the primary winding of the ignition coil.
Operation (Without Ballast Resistor): In a system without a ballast resistor, the full battery voltage is applied to the primary winding. This can cause the coil to overheat and fail.

Operation (With Ballast Resistor): The ballast resistor reduces the voltage applied to the coil's primary winding during normal operation. During engine cranking, the ballast resistor is bypassed, providing a higher voltage to the coil for a stronger spark. This is required because the battery voltage drops during cranking.

cards.title: Operation in Ignition System — Components, Operation & Diagnosis
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Primary: When the ignition switch is turned on, battery voltage flows through the primary winding of the ignition coil.

Breaker Points (or Electronic Trigger): In older systems, the distributor's breaker points open and close, interrupting the primary circuit. In electronic systems, a trigger mechanism (inductive, Hall effect, or optical) performs this function.
Induction: When the primary circuit is interrupted, the magnetic field in the coil collapses.
Secondary: The collapsing magnetic field induces a high voltage in the secondary winding of the coil.
Distributor (or Direct Ignition): The distributor's rotor directs the high voltage spark to the appropriate spark plug. In modern direct ignition systems, each spark plug has its own coil.
Spark Plug Ignition: The high-voltage spark jumps the gap between the spark plug electrodes, igniting the air-fuel mixture.

cards.title: Construction in Ignition System — Components, Operation & Diagnosis
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Battery: Provides the initial low-voltage power.
Ignition Switch: Controls the flow of power to the ignition system.
Ignition Coil: A transformer that steps up the battery voltage to a high voltage (typically 12,000 to 45,000 volts).
Distributor (Older Systems): Contains a mechanical breaker point assembly (or electronic pickup) and a rotor. It distributes the high voltage spark to the correct spark plug at the correct time.
Spark Plugs: Create the spark gap in the combustion chamber.

cards.title: Inductive Type (Magnetic Pickup)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Consists of a reluctor (a toothed wheel) mounted on the distributor shaft and a magnetic pickup coil.

Explanation: Operation: As the reluctor teeth pass the pickup coil, they induce a voltage pulse in the coil. The pulses are then used to trigger the ignition module, which controls the primary circuit of the ignition coil.

Explanation: The reluctor teeth alter the magnetic field of the pickup coil as they pass. This change in magnetic flux induces a voltage in the coil. The frequency of the pulses is proportional to the engine speed.

cards.title: Hall Generator (Hall Effect Sensor)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Consists of a rotating trigger wheel with slots or vanes and a Hall effect sensor.

Explanation: Operation: The Hall effect sensor generates a voltage when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to its current flow. The trigger wheel interrupts the magnetic field as it rotates, creating voltage pulses. These pulses are used to trigger the ignition module.

Explanation: The Hall effect sensor uses a semiconductor material that generates a voltage when placed in a magnetic field. When the trigger wheel rotates, the slots or vanes interrupt the magnetic field, causing the sensor to produce voltage pulses. These pulses are very precise.

cards.title: Optical Pulse (Optical Sensor)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Consists of a rotating trigger wheel with slots or holes, an LED (light-emitting diode), and a phototransistor.

Explanation: Operation: The LED emits a light beam that is interrupted by the slots or holes in the trigger wheel. The phototransistor detects the light pulses and converts them into electrical pulses. These pulses are used to trigger the ignition module.

Explanation: The optical sensor uses light to detect the position of the trigger wheel. The LED emits a light beam, and the phototransistor detects the presence or absence of light. As the trigger wheel rotates, the slots or holes interrupt the light beam, creating pulses. These pulses are very accurate and immune to electromagnetic interference.

cards.title: Distributor Type Electronic Ignition
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Retains a distributor for spark distribution. Uses an electronic trigger (inductive, Hall effect, or optical) instead of mechanical breaker points. An ignition module controls the primary circuit of the coil. High voltage coil.

Explanation: Layout: The electronic trigger is located inside the distributor. The ignition module is typically mounted on the distributor or elsewhere in the engine compartment. The coil is connected to the distributor and the ignition module.

Explanation: Operation: The electronic trigger generates pulses based on the distributor shaft's rotation. The ignition module receives these pulses and controls the primary circuit of the ignition coil. When the primary circuit is interrupted, the coil produces a high voltage spark. The distributor rotor distributes the spark to the appropriate spark plug.

cards.title: Distributorless Ignition System (DIS)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Eliminates the distributor. Uses a crankshaft position sensor and a camshaft position sensor to determine engine position. Uses a coil pack with multiple coils, each serving two cylinders. An engine control unit (ECU) controls the ignition timing.
Explanation: Layout: Sensors are located on the crankshaft and camshaft. The coil pack is mounted on the engine. The ECU is located in the engine compartment or under the dashboard.

Explanation: Operation: The sensors provide engine position information to the ECU. The ECU calculates the optimal ignition timing and triggers the appropriate coils in the coil pack. Each coil fires two spark plugs simultaneously, one during the compression stroke and the other during the exhaust stroke (wasted spark system).

cards.title: Direct Ignition System (DIS or Coil-on-Plug)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Eliminates the distributor and coil pack. Uses individual ignition coils mounted directly on each spark plug. An ECU controls the ignition timing. Crankshaft and camshaft sensors.
Explanation: Layout: Sensors are located on the crankshaft and camshaft. Coils are mounted directly on the spark plugs. The ECU is located in the engine compartment or under the dashboard.

Explanation: Operation: The sensors provide engine position information to the ECU. The ECU calculates the optimal ignition timing and triggers each coil independently. Each coil fires only one spark plug.

cards.title: Capacitor Discharge Ignition (CDI)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Uses a capacitor to store electrical energy. Uses a trigger mechanism (inductive, Hall effect, or optical) to control the discharge of the capacitor. Uses a step-up transformer to produce a high-voltage spark.
Explanation: Layout: The capacitor, trigger mechanism, and transformer are typically housed in a single unit.

Explanation: Operation: The capacitor is charged by a charging circuit. When the trigger mechanism activates, the capacitor discharges rapidly through the primary winding of the transformer. The transformer steps up the voltage, producing a high-voltage spark.

cards.title: Energy Transfer Ignition
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Uses two coils: a primary coil and a secondary coil. The primary coil stores energy, and the secondary coil transfers it to the spark plug. Triggering mechanism.
Explanation: Layout: The coils and trigger mechanism are typically housed in a single unit.

Explanation: Operation: The primary coil stores energy when the primary circuit is closed. When the primary circuit is opened, the energy is transferred to the secondary coil. The secondary coil produces a high-voltage spark that is delivered to the spark plug.

blocks.body: Construction: Uses two coils: a primary coil and a secondary coil. The primary coil stores energy, and the secondary coil transfers it to the spark plug. Triggering mechanism.
Layout: The coils and trigger mechanism are typically housed in a single unit.

Operation: The primary coil stores energy when the primary circuit is closed. When the primary circuit is opened, the energy is transferred to the secondary coil. The secondary coil produces a high-voltage spark that is delivered to the spark plug.

cards.title: Reasons for Differences
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Heat Range (Cold/Hot): The heat range of a spark plug is determined by its ability to dissipate heat. Cold plugs dissipate heat quickly, preventing pre-ignition in high-performance engines. Hot plugs retain more heat, burning off deposits and preventing fouling in standard engines.

Explanation: Reach (Short/Long): The reach of a spark plug is determined by the length of its threaded section. This difference is dictated by the design of the cylinder head. Using the correct reach ensures that the firing tip is positioned correctly within the combustion chamber for optimal ignition.

polytechnic/nc-auto/ignition-starting-ch.title: Magnetism, Motors & Starter Systems
snippets: Complete guide to magnetism principles, generators, DC motors, starter motor types, relays, and keyless start systems.

Moving electric charges create magnetic fields. These fields exert a force on other moving charges or magnetic materials. Magnetic fields are visualised as lines of force, which form closed loops around the source of the magnetic field.
Magnets have two poles: a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel each other (north-north or south-south), and unlike poles attract each other (north-south).
Certain materials, like iron, nickel, and cobalt, are strongly attracted to magnets. These are called ferromagnetic materials. Other materials are weakly attracted or repelled by magnets.

cards.title: Generator Principle (Electromagnetic Induction)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: The generator principle is based on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction. This law states that:
A changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force (EMF) or voltage in a conductor.
The magnitude of the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of the magnetic flux linking the conductor.
In simpler terms, when a conductor moves through a magnetic field or when a magnetic field changes around a conductor, a voltage is generated.

cards.title: DC Generators (Dynamos)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Operation: The armature rotates within a stationary magnetic field. A commutator is used to convert the AC generated in the armature into DC.

Definition: Commutation: The commutator is a split ring that reverses the connections between the armature and the external circuit every half rotation. This ensures that the current flowing through the external circuit is always in the same direction.

Explanation: Polarisation: In older DC generators, residual magnetism in the field windings is essential for starting the generation process. This residual magnetism initiates a small current, which strengthens the field windings, leading to increased output. Modern generators utilise permanent magnets, or electronic controls to provide the initial field.

cards.title: Motor Principle in Magnetism, Motors & Starter Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: The motor principle is based on the interaction between a magnetic field and a current-carrying conductor. When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This force causes the conductor to move.
Definition: This principle is the inverse of the generator principle.

Explanation: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule: This rule helps determine the direction of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field. The thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the left hand are extended at right angles to each other. The forefinger represents the magnetic field, the middle finger represents the current, and the thumb represents the motion (force).

cards.title: Change-Over Relay (SPDT Relay)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Function: A change-over relay is a Single Pole Double Throw (SPDT) relay. It has one common terminal and two output terminals. Its purpose is to switch between two different circuits or functions based on the relay's state (energised or de-energised).

Explanation: Operation: When the relay is de-energised, the common terminal is connected to one of the output terminals (normally closed, NC). When the relay is energised, the common terminal switches and connects to the other output terminal (normally open, NO).
Explanation: Example: A change-over relay could be used to disable the vehicle's headlights while the starter motor is engaged, thus providing more power to the starter.

cards.title: Electromagnetism in Magnetism, Motors & Starter Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: This is the magnetism produced by an electric current. When an electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. The strength of the magnetic field is proportional to the current. An electromagnet consists of a coil of wire wrapped around a ferromagnetic core. When current flows through the coil, it creates a strong magnetic field. Electromagnets are used in various applications, such as electric motors, generators, and solenoids.

cards.title: Electromagnetic Induction in Magnetism, Motors & Starter Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: This is the phenomenon where a changing magnetic field induces an electric current in a conductor. If a conductor is moved through a magnetic field or if a magnetic field changes around a conductor, a voltage (electromotive force or EMF) is induced in the conductor. This principle is the basis for electric generators, transformers, and many other electrical devices. Essentially, if a magnetic field lines "cut" across a conductor, or if a conductor "cuts" across magnetic field lines, then a voltage is induced within that conductor.

cards.title: Key Fob and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: The system relies on a key fob, which contains a small transmitter.
The fob emits a low-frequency radio signal that communicates with the vehicle's electronic control unit (ECU).
The vehicle has antennas that detect the fob's signal.
When the fob is within a certain range of the vehicle (typically a few feet), the vehicle's system recognises its presence.
This communication uses RFID technology, which allows for secure authentication.

cards.title: Start Button Operation
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: After successful authentication, the driver can press the start button to start the engine.
The start button typically sends a signal to the ECU, which then engages the starter motor.
The ECU controls the starting process, including the engagement of the starter motor and the timing of the ignition and fuel injection systems.
Some vehicles require the driver to press the brake pedal or clutch pedal simultaneously with the start button for safety reasons.
The system can also control other vehicle functions, such as unlocking the doors, adjusting the seats, and setting the climate control.

cards.title: Power Factor (PF)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Ratio of real power (watts) to apparent power (volt-amperes). Indicates how effectively electrical power is used.
PF = 1 (100%) in purely resistive circuit (voltage and current in phase).
PF = 0 in purely inductive or capacitive circuit (90° out of phase).
PF is between 0 and 1 in circuits with both resistance and reactance.
Significance: Low PF indicates poor power usage, increased current, voltage drops, and energy losses.
Power Factor Correction: Using capacitors to improve efficiency.

cards.title: Self-Excitation in AC Production & Charging Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Most common method in modern automotive alternators.
Residual magnetism in rotor/field windings initiates the process.
As alternator starts rotating, a small voltage is induced in stator.
This voltage is rectified and used to increase current in field windings, strengthening the magnetic field.
Process continues until desired output voltage is reached.
Efficient and eliminates need for external power source.

cards.title: Operational Details in AC Production & Charging Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Battery State of Charge (SOC) Monitoring: ECU monitors SOC. If low, increases alternator output. When fully charged, reduces or suspends output to minimise parasitic losses.
Load Management: ECU considers electrical load. During high demand (headlights, heated seats), increases output. During low demand, reduces output.
Regenerative Braking Integration: In hybrid/electric vehicles, increases alternator output during deceleration to convert kinetic energy to electrical energy stored in battery.
Temperature Compensation: Adjusts charging voltage based on battery temperature (higher voltage for cold, lower for warm).
Fuel Efficiency Optimisation: Reduces alternator load when possible (during acceleration). Increases output during coasting/deceleration.
Communication: ECU communicates with smart alternator via LIN or CAN bus for precise control.

cards.title: Mechanical Generation (Alternator)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Imagine a loop of wire rotating within a uniform magnetic field.
As the loop rotates, the angle between the loop and the magnetic field lines continuously changes.
The induced voltage in the loop is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux, which is highest when the loop is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel.
This results in a sinusoidal voltage waveform.
One complete rotation of the loop corresponds to one cycle of the sine wave.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Current Limitation: Resistors always limit current flow, impacting the inductor's behaviour.
Phase Shift Reduction: In a purely inductive circuit, current lags voltage by 90°. Adding a resistor reduces this phase shift to less than 90°.
Impedance: Z = √(R² + X L ²)
Power Dissipation: Resistor dissipates power as heat, reducing efficiency.
Damping: Resistors add damping, reducing oscillations and stabilising the circuit.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details

Time Constant: τ = R × C determines charging/discharging rate.
Filtering: RC circuits are used as filters; resistor value affects cutoff frequency.

What it is: A large, heavy steel shaft located at the bottom of the engine block. Considered one of the most important moving parts in the entire engine.

What it does: Takes the up-and-down (reciprocating) motion of the pistons and converts it into spinning (rotary) motion. This spinning motion eventually passes through the transmission to the wheels — without it, the engine's power can't move the car.

What it looks like: A long shaft with offset sections called journals (or crank pins) along its length. These journals are slightly off-center from the main axis. From outside you can see the pulley at the front and the flywheel at the back. If opened up, the journals appear as smooth, rounded, polished metal surfaces.

cards.title: Why the Lubrication System Matters
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Reducing friction: Creates a thin oil film between moving parts, minimizing wear.
Cooling: Oil absorbs heat from components and carries it away.
Cleaning: Carries away contaminants (metal particles, combustion byproducts).
Sealing: Helps seal gaps between piston rings and cylinder walls, maintaining compression.
Corrosion prevention: Forms a protective barrier on metal surfaces.

cards.title: Procedure in Drivetrain Components & Transmission
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Prepare the Vehicle: Park on level surface, engage parking brake. Warm up transmission fluid if possible. Safely raise the vehicle.
Locate the Drain Plug: Usually on the bottom of the transmission pan. Consult service manual.
Drain the Old Fluid: Position drain pan, loosen drain plug carefully (fluid may be hot). Allow complete draining. Inspect plug and replace gasket. Reinstall and torque to spec.
Locate the Fill Plug/Dipstick: Usually on side or top of transmission.
Fill with New Fluid: Use funnel, fill to correct level. For automatics, engine running and in park when checking level.
Check for Leaks: Start engine, idle, shift through gears. Inspect drain and fill plugs.

cards.title: Procedure for Bleeding Brakes
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Note: Some ABS systems require special scan tools to bleed properly.
Prepare: Ensure master cylinder full of fresh fluid. Gather wrench, clear tubing, container, fluid.

Attach bleeder hose: To bleeder screw, other end in container partially filled with fluid.
Pump and hold: Assistant pumps pedal several times and holds down.
Open bleeder screw: While pedal held, open screw; air/fluid flows out.
Close bleeder screw: Before pedal reaches floor.

Friction between shoes/pads and drums/rotors slows down wheels.

points: Explanation: Visual: Steering box – metal housing on older/heavy vehicles near front frame. Steering rack – long horizontal metal component in modern vehicles behind engine or front axle.
Explanation: Function: Converts rotational motion of steering wheel into linear motion to turn wheels.
Explanation: Types: Recirculating ball steering box; rack and pinion steering rack.

points: Explanation: Visual: Small belt-driven pump mounted on engine with hoses connected.
Explanation: Function: Provides hydraulic pressure to assist steering.
Explanation: Components: Reservoir for fluid, pump mechanism, pressure hoses.

cards.title: Dampers (Shock Absorbers or Struts)

points: Explanation: Visual: Cylindrical components near each wheel connecting frame/body to suspension.
Explanation: Function: Control suspension movement, absorb shocks/vibrations for smooth ride and tire contact.
Explanation: Types: Shock absorbers (separate from spring); struts (integrated with spring).

cards.title: Ball Joints in Braking, Steering & Suspension Systems
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Function: Connect control arms to steering knuckles, allow multi‑direction movement.
Explanation: Lubrication: If grease fitting, apply grease until old grease purged. Rotate steering wheel while greasing. Inspect dust boots. Sealed units require replacement when play or boot damage.
Explanation: Signs of need: Clunking during turns, loose steering, uneven tire wear.

Explanation: Wheel faults: Bent/damaged rims, loose nuts/bolts, damaged valve stems, worn bearings, imbalance.

cards.title: Elements in Drivetrain & Basic Electricity
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: A pure substance that cannot be broken down by chemical means; made of only one type of atom.

Explanation: Key facts: Basic building blocks of all matter. Organized on periodic table by atomic number (# of protons). Each element has unique properties from atomic structure (electron arrangement).
Explanation: Elements combining into compounds: Through chemical reactions. Example: sodium (reactive metal) + chlorine (poisonous gas) → sodium chloride (table salt).

cards.title: Flow of Current in an Electrical

points: Explanation: For current to flow, three conditions must be met:
Explanation: Simple analogy (water circuit): Pump = voltage source, Pipe = closed circuit, Material = conductor.
A closed circuit (complete path) – continuous loop from power source negative to positive. Any break stops current.
A voltage source (potential difference) – provides the "push" (volts). Without it, no force to drive electrons.
A conductor – material with free electrons (e.g., copper wire).

cards.title: Matter in Drivetrain & Basic Electricity
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Anything that has mass and occupies space (volume). If you can touch it, see it, or feel its presence, it's matter.
Explanation: States of matter: Solid, Liquid, Gas, Plasma – determined by particle arrangement and energy.

Explanation: Why it matters: Everything around us is matter. Mass measures amount, volume measures space. Made of atoms/molecules. Changes in temperature/pressure cause state changes (e.g., ice melting).

cards.title: Step-by-Step Procedure in Drivetrain & Basic Electricity
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Prepare vehicle: Level surface, parking brake, warm fluid (if needed), safely raise.
Locate drain plug: Usually bottom of transmission pan.
Drain old fluid: Position pan, loosen plug (fluid hot), drain completely, clean plug, replace gasket, torque to spec.
Locate fill plug/dipstick: Side or top of transmission.
Fill with new fluid: Use funnel, fill to correct level. For automatics, engine running and in park when checking.
Check for leaks: Start engine, idle, shift through gears, inspect plugs.

Rough/delayed shifts → low fluid, valve body, solenoid failures.
No movement → torque converter, pump, internal failure.
Overheating → low fluid, heavy towing, internal problems.

Torque converter problems → shuddering or failure.

cards.title: Electrical Phenomena, Units, and Formulas
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Electromotive Force (EMF): ε = W / Q (Volts)
Potential Difference (PD): V = W / Q (Volts)
Current: I = Q / t (Amperes)
Resistance (Ohm's Law): R = V / I (Ohms, Ω)
Power: P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R (Watts)
Resistivity: ρ = (R × A) / L (Ω·m)

cards.title: Identifying and Interpreting Key Items
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Cable gauges (AWG): Lower gauge = thicker wire = higher current capacity. Prevents overheating and voltage drop.
Colour codes: North America: black=hot, white=neutral, green=ground. Europe: brown=live, blue=neutral, green/yellow=earth.
Terminal designations (L, N, E, +, −): Ensure correct connections.
Printed circuits (PCBs): Conductive tracks; understanding layout aids troubleshooting.
protection devices: Fuses, circuit breakers – must be correctly rated.
Terminals: Screw, crimp, push-in – choose right type, secure connection.

cards.title: Effects of Electricity
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details

Magnetic effect – magnetic field around conductor (electromagnets, motors, generators).
Chemical effect – electrolysis (electroplating, battery charging).
Light effect – atoms excited emit light (LEDs, fluorescent, arc lamps).
Physiological effect – affects living organisms (pacemakers, defibrillators, electric shocks).

cards.title: Laws Related to Electrical Circuits
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Ohm's Law: V = I × R. Voltage ∝ current (constant temperature).
Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): Total current entering a junction equals total current leaving.
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): Sum of voltages around any closed loop equals zero.
Joule's Law: H = I² × R × t (heat generated).
Power Law: P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R.

polytechnic/nc-auto/wiring-lighting-auxi.title: Warning Devices, Displays & Driver Information Systems
snippets: Complete guide to audible, visual, tactile, textual warnings, sender units, electronic displays (LED, LCD, CRT, VFD, DC EL), and driver information systems (monitoring, trip computer, GPS).
What they are: Devices that produce sound to attract attention.

How they work: Use an electrical signal to vibrate a diaphragm, or produce an oscillating sound wave. The frequency (pitch) and amplitude (loudness) can be varied to create different types of alerts (e.g., different sound for fire vs. security).
What they are: Devices that use light to provide visual alerts.

cards.title: Sensor-Based Sender Units
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: What they are: Units that use sensors to detect changes in physical parameters.
Explanation: How they work: The sensor converts the physical parameter into an electrical signal. The sender unit processes the signal; if abnormal, it activates the warning device.
Temperature sensors — detect changes, trigger alarms if threshold exceeded.
Pressure sensors — monitor pressure levels, trigger alarms if too high or low.
Smoke detectors — detect smoke particles, trigger fire alarms.
Motion sensors — detect movement, trigger security alarms.
Fluid level sensors — detect high/low fluid levels in tanks.

Explanation: Common types: Emergency stop buttons, fire alarm pull stations, panic buttons.
Explanation: How they work: When activated, opens or closes an electrical circuit, triggering the warning device.

cards.title: Control System Sender Units
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: What they are: Sender units integrated into larger control systems.
Explanation: How they work: Monitor various parameters continuously; trigger warnings based on programmed logic. Common in industrial automation and building management systems.
Explanation: Example: A PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) monitors multiple sensor inputs; if a certain combination occurs, it activates a warning light and a siren.

cards.title: LED (Light-Emitting Diode)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: A semiconductor diode that emits light when current flows. Consists of a p-n junction (e.g., gallium arsenide phosphide). When forward-biased, electrons and holes recombine, releasing energy as photons. Color depends on semiconductor material.
Explanation: Operation: When voltage applied, electrons move from n-type to p-type, holes opposite. Recombination releases light. Intensity proportional to current.
Explanation: Advantages: Energy-efficient, long lifespan, many colors available.

cards.title: Global Positioning System (GPS)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details

Used for navigation (turn-by-turn), location tracking, mapping. Modern systems combine with mapping software and real-time traffic data.
Explanation: Purpose: Provide accurate navigation; enhance safety and security; provide location-based services.

cards.title: Cathode Ray Tube (CRT)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Vacuum tube with electron gun and phosphor-coated screen. Electromagnetic fields steer the electron beam.

Explanation: Operation: Electron gun fires beam toward screen; deflection coils control direction to scan across screen. Beam intensity determines brightness. (Widely used in older TVs/monitors, now largely replaced.)

cards.title: LCD (Liquid Crystal Display)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Liquid crystal material sandwiched between two glass plates with polarizing filters and electrodes. Backlight often used.

Explanation: Operation: When electric field applied, liquid crystal molecules align, changing polarization of light. By controlling the field, individual pixels turn on/off, creating images. Used in laptops, smartphones, TVs, etc.

cards.title: Vacuum Fluorescent Display (VFD)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Vacuum tube with cathode, grid, and anode (phosphor-coated).

Explanation: Operation: Cathode emits electrons; grid controls them; electrons strike phosphor-coated anode, causing it to glow. Bright, wide viewing angle; common in car stereos and industrial displays.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Construction: Phosphor layer sandwiched between two electrodes, often with a dielectric layer.
Explanation: Operation: When DC voltage applied, phosphor emits light via electroluminescence. Thin profile, uniform emission. Less common than other technologies.
