cards.title: Compound Fertilisers in Soil And Water
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Fertilisers that contain two or three major nutrients (N, P, K) in a single mixture.
Examples: NPK 10-20-10 (10% N, 20% P₂O₅, 10% K₂O).
LAN 28% (limestone ammonium nitrate – N only, but often blended).
Use: Convenient for general fertilisation. Often tailored for specific crops (e.g., maize, tobacco).
Commercial farmers in Zimbabwe use a mix of organic and inorganic fertilisers. Compound fertilisers like Compound D (8-14-7) and Compound C (7-14-8) are common for maize and tobacco.

Small‑scale farmers often rely on cattle manure and compost because they are cheaper and improve soil structure. Government programmes like Pfumvudza (conservation agriculture) promote the use of organic and inorganic fertilisers together.

cards.title: Soil And Water: What to Remember
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: • Soil profile has six horizons (O, A, E, B, C, R). Each has different composition and significance for crop growth – the A horizon is the most fertile.
• Soil types – sand (gritty, drains quickly), clay (sticky, holds water/nutrients), loam (mixture, ideal for most crops). Loam is best for farming.
• Fertilisers – organic (manure, compost) improves structure; inorganic (chemical) gives quick nutrients. Straight fertilisers have N, P, or K alone; compound fertilisers have blends like NPK.

• Irrigation is essential for reliable production. Water sources include surface water (rivers, dams), groundwater (boreholes), and rainwater. Water quality (salinity, pH, sodium) must be checked to avoid crop damage.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Christianity is based on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. Christians believe that Jesus is the Son of God and the Saviour of the world. Here are the key beliefs:
Symbols: Star of David, Menorah, Mezuzah
Belief in One God: Christians believe in one God who is the creator of the universe. They believe that God is love and that He cares for all people.
The Trinity: Christians believe that God exists in three persons in one – God the Father, God the Son (Jesus Christ), and God the Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity.

Jesus Christ as Saviour: Christians believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and the Messiah. They believe that Jesus died on the cross to save people from their sins, and that He rose from the dead on the third day.

cards.title: Belief in Other Spirits
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Indigenous Religion also believes in other spirits that live in nature. These spirits can be good or bad, and they are found in rivers, mountains, trees, and animals.
Some spirits are called mashave (in Shona) or amahlozi (in Ndebele). These are spirits that are not ancestors but can influence people's lives.
Some people are believed to have special relationships with these spirits and can communicate with them. These people are called spirit mediums or traditional healers.
Fire: Fire is an important symbol in Indigenous Religion. It represents purity, communication with ancestors, and spiritual presence. Fire is used in ceremonies and rituals.
Rivers and water: Water is seen as a source of life and purification. Many rituals are performed near rivers or using water from rivers.
Sacred trees: Some trees, such as the baobab or the mutiti tree, are considered sacred. They are places where ancestors are believed to dwell.

cards.title: Totems in Religion in Zimbabwe
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: A totem is an animal, bird, or plant that represents a clan or family. The Shona call totems mitupo, and the Ndebele call them izibongo.
Totems are usually animals like the zebra, lion, monkey, fish, or the pangolin. Each clan has its own totem.
Purpose of totems: They identify people and show which clan they belong to.
They connect people to their ancestors.
They create a sense of belonging and unity within the clan.
They prevent people from marrying someone from the same clan (exogamy).

cards.title: Taboos in Religion in Zimbabwe
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: A taboo is something that is forbidden or not allowed. Taboos are rules that people must follow to avoid offending the spirits or bringing bad luck. The Shona call taboos zviramu (or zviera ).
Examples of taboos: Eating the animal that is your totem.
Marrying someone from the same clan.
Pointing at graves or sacred places.
Killing or harming animals that are considered sacred.
Purpose of taboos: They protect people from harm and misfortune.

cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Ancestral spirits are the spirits of people who have died. They are believed to watch over their living relatives and help them in times of need.
Ancestors are seen as intermediaries between the living and the Supreme Being. People communicate with them through prayer, offerings, and rituals.

Ancestors are honoured and respected. They are believed to punish those who break traditional customs and reward those who follow them.

cards.title: Gender Roles in Religion and Contemporary Issues
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Definition: Unhu (in Shona) or Ubuntu (in Ndebele) is a philosophy that guides how people should behave. It is about being a good person and treating others with kindness and respect. Unhu is not just about following rules – it is about having a good heart and caring for others.
Explanation: In Zimbabwe, different religions have different beliefs about health and sickness. These beliefs affect how people understand illness and what they do about it.
At home: boys – strength, girls – caregiving
Christianity: varies – from traditional to equality
Islam: equal before God, different roles

What is right conduct? Right conduct means doing things that help others and do not harm anyone. It includes showing respect for elders, being honest, helping people in need, and living in peace with others.
What is wrong conduct? Wrong conduct means doing things that hurt others or go against the values of the community. It includes lying, stealing, cheating, disrespecting elders, and causing harm.

Why does Unhu matter? Unhu is what makes a person truly human. A person who does not care about others is not seen as a good person. Unhu teaches that we are all connected, and that our actions affect others.

points: Explanation: The Constitution of Zimbabwe protects the rights of all people. These rights are based on human dignity and respect for all individuals. Here are some of the basic rights included in the Constitution:

Definition: Social responsibility is the duty of every person to act in ways that benefit society. It means caring about the well‑being of others and the community. Religion encourages social responsibility in many ways:
IR: totems protect animals, sacred places protect land
Taboos: protect water, trees, and cleanliness
Christianity: sometimes has harmed, but now embracing creation care
Right to life: Everyone has the right to life. No one should be killed unjustly. This right protects people from murder, violence, and the death penalty.
Right to human dignity: Every person has the right to be treated with respect. No one should be humiliated, tortured, or treated in a degrading way.
Right to education: Everyone has the right to education. Primary education is compulsory for all children. This helps people develop and improve their lives.

Explanation: These roles can be different in different families and communities. Some families are more flexible, while others follow traditional roles very strictly.

cards.title: African Independent Churches
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: African Independent Churches (AICs) are churches that were started by African people, separate from mission churches. Many of these churches supported the liberation struggle.
The Zionist Church and African Apostolic Church were important. Their leaders often encouraged their members to support the freedom fighters.
Some church leaders used their knowledge of the land and their connections to the community to help the fighters. They provided food, shelter, and information.
Many AICs believed that the struggle for independence was part of God's plan and that they were fighting for justice.

blocks.title: Key points about African Independent Churches
items: African Independent Churches (AICs) are churches that were started by African people, separate from mission churches. Many of these churches supported the liberation struggle.
The Zionist Church and African Apostolic Church were important. Their leaders often encouraged their members to support the freedom fighters.
Some church leaders used their knowledge of the land and their connections to the community to help the fighters. They provided food, shelter, and information.

cards.title: Mission Churches (Roman Catholic, Anglican, Methodist, etc.)
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Mission churches also played a role in the liberation struggle, although in different ways. Some missionaries and church leaders supported the struggle, while others were against it.
Some church leaders spoke out against the injustices of the colonial system. They called for equality and justice for all people.
Some missionaries provided medical care and education to the people, which was a form of support and helped the community resist oppression.
The Roman Catholic Church in Zimbabwe had leaders who supported the freedom fighters and spoke out against the government's violence.

cards.title: Indigenous Religion in Religion and Contemporary Issues
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: In Indigenous Religion, men are often seen as the leaders of the family and the community. They are responsible for protecting the family and representing them in religious ceremonies.
Women are respected as mothers and caregivers. They are responsible for raising children and managing the household. Some women are also spiritual leaders, such as spirit mediums.
There is a balance between men and women. Both are valued for their different roles and contributions.

cards.title: Christianity in Religion and Contemporary Issues
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Some Christian traditions teach that men are the heads of the household and that women should be submissive to their husbands. This is based on some passages in the Bible.
Other Christian denominations, especially more modern ones, teach that men and women are equal and can both lead and serve in the church. In many churches today, women are pastors and leaders.
Christianity has also influenced gender roles by challenging harmful practices like violence against women and promoting education for girls.

cards.title: Islam in Religion and Contemporary Issues
cards.subtitle: Understand the idea, then remember the details
points: Explanation: Today, many people are rethinking traditional gender roles. Both men and women are realising that they can do many different things. Religion can be a source of support for equality, but it can also be used to justify inequality. It is important to look at each religion's teachings carefully and to think about how they apply to modern life.

In Islam, men and women are considered equal before God, but they have different roles in life. Men are often seen as the providers and protectors, while women are seen as the caregivers and managers of the home.
Muslim women are valued for their role as mothers and are respected in the community. Many Muslim women also work outside the home and contribute to the family's income.
